entries.section: (5) With the commu

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah: a Hebrew name meaning "God has comforted."
Chislev: corresponds to the month of December.
The twentieth year: the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, king of the kingdom of Media and Persia, which ruled the world at that time.
Shushan the palace: the capital of Media and Persia, located in the south-west of Persia, that is, present-day Iran, 200 miles east of Babylon.

Nehemiah, the writer of this book, specifies the place and time of the events that follow in this chapter: while Nehemiah was in the city of Shushan the palace, in the month of Chislev, what is told in the following verses took place.

entries.section: (5) With the commu

paragraphs.text: The Jews: the people of God used to be called the Hebrews, after Abraham who crossed the river Euphrates and lived in Canaan. But after the captivity the people were called Jews, after the tribe of Judah, which represented the southern kingdom that was taken captive after the northern kingdom. When the people of God returned, they returned as one undivided kingdom, and all of them were called Jews.

Nehemiah's concern for his people and his city Jerusalem is evident: his position in the royal palace did not distract him from caring about the news of those who dwelt in Jerusalem. Perhaps he went out of the palace at this time and met one of his relatives according to the flesh, named Hanani, and he calls him "my brother" because he was of the same tribe, the tribe of Levi. Hanani and some of the Jews were returning from a journey to Jerusalem, where they had visited their homeland and their relatives, so Nehemiah asked them about the Jews living in Jerusalem who had escaped death during the Babylonian attack in which the inhabitants of Jerusalem were taken captive.

May you care for your relatives and loved ones, especially the weak, for they are the ones in need, so that you ask about their news and try to help them. Do not let the concerns of life and your own needs distract you from your needy brethren.

entries.section: (5) With the commu

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah heard bad news about the Jews who remained in Jerusalem: that they were in weakness and misery, because the walls of Jerusalem were still broken down since the Babylonian attack and its great gates were burned with fire. That is, the city was without protection and the people living in it were exposed to attack by any enemy. They were also in shame and disgrace, because all the surrounding cities and neighboring lands were fortified with strong walls and gates, as was the custom of that time; that is, Jerusalem had become a despised and humiliated city, and this had lasted for 140 years since the days of the Babylonian attack.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: When Nehemiah heard the news of the ruined Jerusalem, he entered his chamber and sat quietly before God. He felt sorrow, not over Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of the walls and the city, because this had been known for a long time, but he was grieved, and even wept, over his sense of his own failure and the failure of all the Jews toward their God and His holy city Jerusalem, in which stood the temple of God, the holiest place in the world. Perhaps he asked himself, how can I live in a great palace while the holy city's walls are broken down?

He found nothing before him but to take refuge in God in fasting, declaring his readiness to strip himself of all the material things he enjoyed for God's sake. He came forward to pray in contrition and supplication to God, that He might help him and help all who love God and believe in Him, so that they might care for His holy city Jerusalem.

Nehemiah continued in his seclusion, fasting, prayers and tears for days. This was not a passing emotion but deep feelings asking God for help, so that they might be turned into strong works that please Him. The number of days he spent in seclusion is not mentioned, but it is clear that it was not a short period, spent in private seclusion with God away from the eyes of people, because his hope was firm in God, who alone is able to do all things.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: The God of heaven: an expression for God used after the Babylonian captivity, which destroyed the temple, because this expression proclaims God's dwelling place, which cannot be destroyed, namely heaven.

Nehemiah began his prayer, which continues to the end of this chapter, declaring in reverence that he stood before the great God, the God of heaven, to distinguish Him from the pagan gods on earth, and because God is the only God and is feared by all His creation for His greatness and majesty.

At the same time He is a compassionate God who cares for His children who believe in Him, who keep His commandments and hold fast to His covenants. He never forsakes them but shepherds them and upholds them if they take refuge in Him. So Nehemiah here seeks God's mercies, that He may have compassion on him and on all his brethren the Jews, His people who worship Him and need His help to build His holy city.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: In humility he raised his voice before God, feeling his unworthiness because of the multitude of his sins. As one responsible for his people, he came before God on their behalf, bearing their sins and entreating Him, confessing the neglect of building the holy city, although he had not been with them, and those who had fallen short were the Jews living in Jerusalem; but as a true servant he offered repentance for all his people. And because he was unworthy, he entreated God to allow Him to open His ear to hear his prayer and to look with His eyes upon the humiliation of his people. For though they were unworthy, they were His needy children, and he was confident of His fatherhood, which never forsakes them. He borrows the ear and the eye and ascribes them to God, to express the extent of his faith in the God who was before him and his great need of His intervention.

Nehemiah was not charged with the responsibility of building Jerusalem, but out of his love for God and for His city he felt responsible. Perhaps he realized at that time that God might have permitted him this great position in the royal palace so that he might serve God and build His city. He kept repeating these words in different phrases and expressions throughout the days of his seclusion, insistently asking for God's intervention. Indeed, the day was not enough for him to pray, but he spent a long part of the night in vigil, with supplications and tears, that God might have mercy on him and on all his people.

Nehemiah is an example of the spiritual man whose heart is attached to God more than to all the material things around him, who feels for his brethren before himself, and for the glory of God before any personal benefit, so that he had these deep feelings while far from Jerusalem, whereas most of those who lived in Jerusalem felt nothing of these feelings.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: We have dealt corruptly: we committed sins that corrupted our life and separated us from God.

Nehemiah remembered the sins of his people over tens of years, which led to God's discipline of them by captivity and the burning of the temple. So today he comes forward declaring that the cause of the broken walls and the burned gates is their sins. He speaks in the first person plural, declaring his responsibility for all the evils his people did, and for the failures in worshiping God and keeping His commandments, which they received at the hand of Moses the prophet.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: He reminds God of His promises in His Law (Deut 30:1-5): that if His people forsook His commandments and worshiped idols, that is, betrayed God, He would scatter them and disperse them among the peoples, and this indeed happened in the captivity. But he completes his words by reminding God of His promises that if they repented and returned to Him, He would gather them from their dispersion, even if they were in all parts of the world, and bring them back to their land to worship Him in His holy temple in Jerusalem, where God chose this place for His dwelling.
When he says "remember," this does not mean that God has forgotten, but Nehemiah declares his faith in God's Law and holds Him to His promises, and this rejoices God's heart.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: He reminds God that the Jews are His people whom He chose from among all peoples because they believed in Him and worshiped Him, and that He saved them and redeemed them from the hands of the Egyptians by the slaying of the Passover lamb, by whose blood He saved their firstborn from death, delivered them and brought them out of Egypt, and parted the Red Sea before them and brought them across, at the time when the firstborn of Egypt were killed and Pharaoh and all his army were drowned. And this is, of course, a type of Christ, the Redeemer of mankind.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah's prayer

paragraphs.text: At the end of the prayer he repeated his petition that God would hear his prayer and even give him favor before the king whom Nehemiah served, for he was working as cupbearer to the king, which is a high position with a large number of workers under it. For, by God's guidance, many ideas came to his mind by which he could build the broken walls, and they needed the king's approval, and he was confident that God was able to persuade the king to agree to all his requests, so that he would succeed in building the walls.

And in faith Nehemiah trusted that there were believing Jews, whether in Jerusalem, or with him in Shushan the palace, or throughout the kingdom, who cared about Jerusalem and were praying to God for its rebuilding and the building of its walls. Perhaps this feeling reached him not only from his brethren the Jews who told him about Jerusalem, but he sensed by God's guidance that there were others who lifted up prayer before God, and this shows the extent of Nehemiah's faith, for he did not despair and did not feel that he was alone, as Elijah felt long ago (1 Kgs 18:22). Nehemiah held the position of the king's cupbearer, and whether he was the chief of the cupbearers or one of the senior cupbearers who stood before the king, it is a position of special standing, because he was near the king at all times, whether during his work or his rest, whenever he needed to drink. This allowed a very close personal relationship and friendship with the king. He was entrusted with the king's life, since he would pour drops of the drink, whether wine or another, into the palm of his left hand and taste them before the king, to assure the king that the drink was free of poison, thereby declaring his readiness to redeem the king's life from any harm. The position of Nehemiah was already discussed in the introduction to this book. And we see in this prayer Nehemiah's faith, which appeared in his calling on God to intervene, as follows:
1- Reminding Him of what He said in His Law and of His promise to gather His scattered people if they repented and returned to Him.
2- That God is able to build these walls, just as He rescued His people long ago from the bondage of Egypt and redeemed them.
3- That the people of God are His servants, who keep His commandments and love Him, that is, they are His own, whom He must intervene to support.

4- That His people want to live in His fear, for they strive spiritually to please Him, and He never forsakes those who draw near to Him, even if they are weak and fall short, so long as they want to please Him. He helps them to worship Him faithfully and builds the holy city for them, so that they may be at ease and practice their worship in all freedom in His holy temple.

God greatly rejoices when you draw near to Him and in your earnest prayer toward Him. So place your problems before God every day and be insistent with Him, and do not leave Him, confident that He rejoices in your prayers and never forsakes you, and that He works miracles to bring about your good, so that you live with Him forever.
The king sends Nehemiah to build the walls

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: The month of Nisan: corresponds to the month of April.

The twentieth year: the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes. Its beginning is not tied to the beginning of the civil year but starts in one of its months. Four months passed between the months of Chislev and Nisan (December and April), from Nehemiah's hearing the news of the ruined Jerusalem to his coming before the king mentioned in this chapter.
Sad (of countenance): a manifestation of deep grief on the face.

A large number of cupbearers worked for the king, each with his own turn. Every few or several months the cupbearer's turn comes to take care of serving drinks to the king. Four months passed between the events of the first chapter and this chapter, and this shows that the days Nehemiah spent in his seclusion, which are referred to simply as days, took a period that was not short, which may have extended to a month or two in retreat. When Nehemiah's turn came to serve wine and drinks to the king, four months had passed since he had heard the news of the broken walls and the burned gates, and the sorrow of his heart was so deep that it showed on his face throughout this period, and he could not hide it when he came before the king, although it was dangerous for the cupbearer to appear with sorrow on his face, lest the king be angry, especially since Nehemiah was a spiritual man who believed in God, so the cheerfulness of his face was clear and expressed his deep joy, and therefore a great difference showed when his face was sad.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: When the king noticed the signs of sorrow on Nehemiah's face, he asked him the reason for his sorrow although he was not sick, because sickness sometimes causes pains that make the face sad. Then the king continued, saying that these signs of sorrow show that your heart is sad. So Nehemiah was afraid, because it was customary at that time for the king's personal attendants to appear before him with joy and a smile, and if they appeared otherwise they were liable to be put to death.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah answered the king with the greeting and honor customary at that time, praying that he might live forever. Then he told him the reason for the sadness of his face, which was his discovery that the city of his fathers, in which their tombs are located, was in ruins, without walls, and that its gates were burned. The ancients prized the tombs of their fathers, and it grieved them that these should not be under protection inside fortified cities, and that any tampering with these tombs insulted them and distressed them greatly. By this Nehemiah aroused the king's sympathy with him and made him feel his problem and sorrows. He did not say to the king that he wanted to build Jerusalem and fortify it, so that the king would not fear the building of fortified cities that might rebel against him one day, but said that it was merely the city of his fathers' tombs, so that he would sympathize with him.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: Here appears God's grace in the king's response to Nehemiah and his readiness to meet his requests to solve his problem, and he even asked him to specify his requests. Here Nehemiah appears as a spiritual man: he lifted his heart in prayer that God might give him wisdom in the eyes of the king and guide him to the requests he should make. Despite his deep prayers and fasts throughout four months, he now prays again in the king's presence that God may speak through his tongue, for the cupbearers were not permitted to ask anything of the king by exploiting their position and their nearness to him. But through prayer Nehemiah believed that God was able to give him favor in the eyes of the king, so that he would grant his requests and not be angry with him.

How beautiful it is that you take refuge in God at all times and in all situations, that He may support you and you experience His power, and on the other hand that you enjoy speaking with God throughout the day and feel the beauty of fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: With courtesy and humility Nehemiah said to the king that if he was pleased with him and felt that his requests were suitable, he would allow him to go to the region of Judah, in which is the land of his fathers and of which Jerusalem is the capital, to build it and repair it because it was in ruins.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: King Artaxerxes was sitting with the queen beside him, and perhaps the queen had a part in the matter of Nehemiah, that is, she spoke with the king in a side conversation to encourage him to sympathize with Nehemiah. It is possible that this queen was Esther, the wife of King Ahasuerus, the father of Artaxerxes, and so she would be his mother, or like a mother to Artaxerxes.

The king agreed to Nehemiah's first request, to allow him to go to Jerusalem to build it, and asked him for the details of his mission, that is, the date of his departure and the length of time he wanted to spend there. By God's guidance Nehemiah specified the period he needed so that the king would grant him this leave from his work as cupbearer. This period was probably months or a year, which he renewed afterward. It is possible that Nehemiah did not stay in Jerusalem the twelve years until it reached him, as is mentioned in this book (ch. 13:6), but he may have returned once or several times to Shushan the palace, and then returned to Jerusalem again.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: Beyond the river: the lands lying around the river Jordan.

Nehemiah presented his second request to the king, which was to obtain letters from the king to the governors under his authority in the region surrounding the Jordan to the east and west, so that they would allow him to pass through their lands until he reached Judah.

entries.section: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

paragraphs.text: The king's forest: the king's gardens with their many trees.
The palace which appertained to the house: a building beside the house, which is the temple of God.
The house that I shall enter into: the dwelling of Nehemiah, who was responsible on behalf of the king for the building of Jerusalem.

After Nehemiah asked the king for leave to travel to Jerusalem (v. 6) and then asked permission to pass through the lands beyond the Jordan (v. 7), he made his third request in this verse, which was for a letter to the keeper of the king's gardens, which are in the region of Jerusalem, so that he might take timber from them to build the palace attached to the temple of God, in which are storerooms and annexes for the service, as well as timber to build the wall of the city and its gates, and finally timber to build a dwelling for Nehemiah himself. So he cares for the temple of God and the city, and in the end asks for what is necessary for himself, namely a dwelling in which to live. He put the building of the palace before the wall so as to show the king his concern for the worship of God in the city where his fathers lived and where their tombs are, and that his concern was not for Jerusalem to be a great and fortified city, so as not to arouse the king's fears about it. By God's grace the king agreed to all of Nehemiah's requests, and Nehemiah felt that he was receiving his requests from the hand of God through the king, for his direct dealing was with God before people. Most likely the king gave to him generously, as God moved him, because it was the good hand of God that gave to Nehemiah, and He is the One "that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not" (Jas 1:5).

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah in Jerusalem and the displeasure of the enemies

paragraphs.text: God's grace appeared with Nehemiah in the king's concern to send soldiers with him to guard him and the few Jews who accompanied him (v. 11). So Nehemiah moved as an official representative of the king, guarded by a military company, which gave him awe in the eyes of the governors beyond the Jordan, and they received him with welcome, especially when they read the king's letters to them. And so he passed through their lands until he arrived at Jerusalem.

God is ready to give you graces from Himself that you did not ask for, and awe in the eyes of those around you. So do not fear the wicked, but use this awe to win everyone for Christ, so that along with their respect for you they see your love and are drawn to your Christ.

entries.section: (2) Nehemiah in Jerusalem and the displeasure of the enemies

paragraphs.text: Sanballat the Horonite: from the city of Horonaim, which lies in the south of Moab and 30 km north-west of Jerusalem. He was a chief and governor in the city of Samaria and hated the Jews, because their strength frightened the Samaritans, so he worked to weaken them.

Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite: he was a servant of the king and at the same time chief of the children of Ammon, who lived east of the Dead Sea. This people were descended from Lot and were hostile to the children of Israel.
It grieved them: a wrong, any matter that saddens and angers.

When the enemies of the children of Israel heard, represented by the leaders of some of the cities and peoples surrounding the people of God, namely Sanballat and Tobiah, they were greatly distressed, because Nehemiah's coming meant good and blessing for Jerusalem and Judah, since whenever Judah was weak these enemies felt their own strength, but if it was strong they feared it.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah arrived at Jerusalem and stayed there three days, examining the city and the walls and learning about all that had happened in it. Nehemiah here is a type of Christ, who stayed three days in the tomb and after this rose from the dead, just as Nehemiah arose to build the city.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: Because of the disgrace in which the ruined Jerusalem lay, Nehemiah set out by night and arose with the small group of Jews who had come with him from Shushan the palace, and they went out on a secret mission to survey the walls and the city. Nehemiah rode on a beast and moved quietly, and he told none of the leaders of Jerusalem about the great work he wished to do, which was building the wall and the city, especially since there were enemies who were concerned that nothing beneficial be done for Jerusalem. Nehemiah was not shaken by their opposition, but he was careful that his mission should be secret, lest he give the enemies an opportunity to increase their opposition.

Great works need examination with patience and calm with oneself before taking great decisions. Calm with prayer and fasting makes you obtain God's mercies and guidance easily. So do not rush into any great matter in your life, but give yourself a chance to hear the voice of God.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: The valley gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, located in its south-west, overlooking the valley of Hinnom adjoining Jerusalem, where the remains of animals and everything left over from the city were thrown and burned with fire, so the fire was always burning in it, and from it the word Gehenna was taken. It is a type of eternal torment, and the valley gate signifies the need for tears and repentance for deliverance from judgment and eternal torment. The dragon well: a statue of a dragon from whose mouth water came out, and this spring was beside the valley gate.

The dung gate: dung is the manure of animals, that is, their waste, because in front of this gate the manure of animals was thrown. So this gate signifies the importance of being cleansed from every impurity, to which the manure thrown far from the city through this gate points. From this point Nehemiah tells in detail how he began to examine the walls of the city, and it is evident that his movement was in the southern part of the city wall, which was the remaining part of the wall, because the enemies' attacks mostly came from the north of the city and its east, so of the wall in these directions only a few traces remained. So he moved from the valley gate toward the dung gate, a distance of about 1 km, and went on examining the broken walls and the burned gates. All this was done by night, away from the eyes of the enemies, so that he might arrange his affairs and take his decisions for rebuilding the wall.
The mention of these two gates signifies the importance of repentance and purity for beginning the spiritual building.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: The fountain gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, located east of the dung gate, beside which is a pool in which the water of the spring near the gate was stored. This pool is called the pool of Siloam or the king's pool because it is near the king's garden, that is, his gardens (2 Kgs 25:4, Jer 52:7). Nehemiah continued examining the wall, so he crossed from the dung gate along the wall to the fountain gate, and there the wall had become so broken down and narrow that he found no place for the beast he was riding to pass. We notice that Nehemiah began examining the wall in the southern part, which had not been broken down as much as the wall in the northern part. He is a positive person who sees the sound part of the wall in some measure before the part that was almost completely broken down, in order to strengthen hope in himself and in those with him.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: After that Nehemiah passed through a valley and went up one of the mountains, because Jerusalem is built on five mountains, and from the mountain he was able to see a considerable part of the wall. Then he returned to where he had begun, that is, to the valley gate.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: The rulers: the leaders of the city of Jerusalem.
The nobles: the great and the rich.

Nehemiah examined the wall with a few of the Jews who had come with him from Shushan the palace, and this mission was completely secret. He told neither the rulers, nor the priests, nor the nobles, nor all the people, as a precaution against the enemies, lest they know his plan and increase their opposition.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: After the secret examination of Jerusalem and its walls, Nehemiah gathered the rulers of the city, its priests, its nobles and its foremen. He told them of the bad state of the city and its walls, so that it had become a disgrace and a reproach among the surrounding lands, in order to arouse their zeal and concern for the holy city. He spoke from study and not merely from news he had heard, so his words were strong and moving to them, and he called them to rise and build the city and its walls.

entries.section: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah also told them about the blessing of God that gave him favor before King Artaxerxes, so that he agreed to his three requests. They rejoiced and took courage and declared their readiness to rise and build. Thus Nehemiah succeeded in encouraging the people and their leaders, for the work is a collective work that all must do, and not one individual, however great his strength.

Care to cooperate with those around you, because collective work is greater than individual works, but it needs study, love for others and encouragement to gather energies, so that God blesses and brings it to completion with success.

entries.section: (4) The enemies' contempt for Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: Geshem the Arabian: one of the chiefs of the tribe of Kedar, which lives in the Arabian peninsula. The enemies of the Jews heard of Nehemiah's words and the people's readiness to build, and they were greatly enraged, because their strength appeared in the weakness of the Jews, and they even tried to exploit the Jews and draw them into following them. So they were distressed at their attempt to gather together and build the city, and thereby become a force that would frighten these enemies. So they sent the first opposition to Nehemiah by accusing him of rebelling against King Artaxerxes in his thought of building the city and its walls. For although Nehemiah had the king's orders and permission to build the city, the enemies frightened him that they were about to send letters to the king accusing him of rebellion, so that he would be shaken and withdraw, for kings do not want disturbances inside the lands subject to them.

entries.section: (4) The enemies' contempt for Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: The strength of Nehemiah's faith appeared in his not being shaken by the enemies' threats, because he relied on God, the God of heaven, who is above every earthly power. He declared with confidence that God would give them success and that they were about to build the city and its walls. Then he declared firmly to the enemies his refusal of any interference from them in the affairs of the Jews, although these enemies, with their influence and their money, had infiltrated and won over many of the Jews to themselves, like Tobiah, who intermarried with the Jewish priests and won over many, so that they made him a place of residence inside the temple of God (ch. 13). Thus appears the strength of faith, which fears neither plots nor the might of enemies.

Have faith in God, who is able to do all things, whatever the oppositions or threats around you, for they are nothing before His power. Hold fast to Him and be insistent with Him in prayers, for He surely does not forsake you and will deliver you from every evil.

The division of the work of building the wall and the gates. The Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, built a wall for the city, then David and Solomon fortified it and completed it, and afterward the Babylonians demolished it when they destroyed Jerusalem and burned it with fire. Now Nehemiah rebuilds the wall and the gates. The gates are twelve; ten of them are mentioned in this chapter, then two in (ch. 12), corresponding to the number of the tribes of the children of Israel, and in the Book of Revelation twelve gates are mentioned for the heavenly Jerusalem, corresponding to the tribes and the disciples of Christ (Rev 21:12). The gate of Ephraim and the prison gate were not mentioned in this chapter, because most likely they did not need repair.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: Malchiah the son of Rechab: he was of the tribe of Rechab, who were not Jews but lived beside them in peace, and Jeremiah mentioned them as an example of obedience to the commands of their chief (Jer 35). The dung gate, as we mentioned in (ch. 2:13), lies south of the city of Jerusalem and east of the valley gate, and the dung of animals was thrown out from it. Therefore this gate signifies purity, that is, a person's being rid of all his evils and impurities, which the waste signifies.
This gate was repaired by one of the great men named Malchiah the son of Rechab, who was ruler of a district called the district of Beth-haccerem.

This shows the concern of the great men for repairing the wall and the gates, and of course the rest of their families followed them, so the work was a popular work in which all the people took part, the great and those who were not great.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The district of Mizpah: a place outside Jerusalem, lying near it, within the tribe of Benjamin.

The fountain gate: called the gate of the spring, and it is opposite En-rogel. We mentioned about it in (2:14) that it lies east of the dung gate and beside it is the pool of Siloam, which was formed from the spring of water, that is, this spring flows into it. The pool of Siloam is in fact an open channel in which the water runs down with a gentle slope and finally flows into a pool called the old pool or the pool of Siloam, which is mentioned in the New Testament, and in which the man born blind washed (Jn 9:6). The spring signifies the Holy Spirit, since no one digs it but it comes forth naturally, just as God's grace gives us the work of the Holy Spirit in us. The spring or the water signifies the sacrament of Baptism, so this gate signifies the Holy Spirit and Baptism.

Shallun repaired this gate, he and his household, then repaired the wall beside this gate as far as the king's garden, called the garden, which is a wide area of gardens belonging to the king, and it extended after that to a stair called the stair of the city of David, and because Jerusalem is built on hills, stairs are many in it. The city of David is a part of Jerusalem called by this name, and sometimes the name city of David is applied to all of Jerusalem. Shallun was ruler of the district of Mizpah, which is a place outside Jerusalem, and this shows the concern of the Jews in all the region of Judea surrounding Jerusalem for repairing the wall of the city of God, just as non-Jews living beside them, such as the Rechabites, also cooperated in this great work.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The district of Beth-zur: a suburb lying outside Jerusalem, 20 miles south of Jerusalem. The sepulchres of David: it was the custom to place tombs outside cities, because whoever touches a dead person becomes unclean, but tombs were set up for the kings, who were of the descendants of David, inside the city of Jerusalem.

The pool that was made: King Hezekiah made it to store water in it after he stopped up the springs outside the city of Jerusalem so that the Assyrians who were besieging his city at that time would not use them.
The house of the mighty: where the military commanders of David's army dwelt, and this area was afterward turned into army barracks and storehouses for weapons.

The complementarity of the two tasks of building the wall appears here: after Shallun, Nehemiah the son of Azbuk repaired the wall opposite the tombs of David, the pool that was made and the house of the mighty. Thus the repair of the wall extends from the south of Jerusalem toward its east as far as the water gate mentioned in (v. 26). By this we find that the direction of the repair began from the north and goes counterclockwise until it finally reaches the north again at the end of this chapter.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: Keilah: a city lying in the plain of Judah near the border of the tribe of Judah with the Philistines. The Levites under Rehum also took part in repairing the wall, as did Hashabiah, who was ruler of the city of Keilah.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: And after Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, his relatives repaired under Bavai, ruler of the other half of the district of Keilah.
That is, all the inhabitants of the city were concerned to take part in this work.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The armory: storehouses of weapons to which the city resorts in time of war.
The turning: a corner in the wall of the city.

A group from the city of Mizpah came forward under one of its rulers, Ezer, to repair a second section of the wall, other than that repaired by their brethren from the city of Mizpah mentioned in (v. 15). This section was opposite a stair at the armory in the corner of the city.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: After the Mizpah group, whom Ezer led, Baruch and those who followed him came forward with great zeal, distinguished from the other groups working in repairing the wall, and he repaired from the corner of the city to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest, that is, the chief of the priests.

May you come forward toward God in earnest worship with care, whether in your prayers or your readings. Make a plan for yourself with your spiritual father and keep to it, and try to seize every opportunity to grow in your worship. This of course will stir your love toward God, and He will reward you with many things, and will open your heart with love for those around you, so that you serve them faithfully and experience new depths in the love of God.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The love of Meremoth and the group with him appears in their concern to repair a second section of the wall other than that which they repaired in (v. 4). This section lies in the eastern part of the temple and extends from the door of the high priest, and of the priests next to him, to the end of these buildings, which were attached to the wall and faced the valley of Kidron, which lies outside Jerusalem.

It is noticed that Meremoth's group were not content to repair the wall opposite their houses, but out of their zeal repaired another part that needed repair, and this shows their activity, which God greatly esteems. What they repaired in (v. 4) was at the fish gate in the north of the city, but the second section in this verse was at the east of the city.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The plain: a depression in the earth, that is, a plain, or a valley, and this name is applied to the southern part of the valley of the river Jordan.

Some of the workers in the temple and some of the priests lived in the plain of the Jordan, that is, the plain surrounding Jerusalem, also called the district, and these priests came and took part in repairing the wall of Jerusalem. This confirms the priests' sense that repairing the wall was a holy work, because it was connected with the holy city Jerusalem, in which was the temple of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: He continues to mention those who took part in the repair, mentioning Benjamin and Hashub, who repaired it, with their followers, opposite their houses, and after them Azariah the son of Maaseiah repaired. This shows that the repair of the wall was a popular work in which every person took part for God's sake, and to protect himself and his city. This signifies the duty of every person to put right any wrongs he meets and to do the good that is available to him, so that he may have a share in the Kingdom of Heaven, becoming a true member of the Church through his love, his service and his doing of good.
When you find an opportunity to do good, do not neglect it, for God is the One who gave it to you so that you may show your love for Him, and so become a true son and obtain His many mercies.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The zeal of some persons in repairing the wall appears here: after they completed the portion assigned to them by Nehemiah, they went back and repaired another section. Among them was Binnui the son of Henadad, mentioned in this verse, who is also called Bavai the son of Henadad, mentioned in (v. 18). In this verse he repaired a part of the wall at a corner in the wall, opposite which was a turning, that is, a small lane that was well known in Jerusalem.

It is noticed that Binnui, or Bavai, is ruler of half the district of Keilah, that is, the rulers were concerned with repairing the wall and not only the people, and this confirms that all classes of the people cared for the work of God.

entries.section: (3) The dung gate and the fountain gate

paragraphs.text: The tower: a tower set up to defend the king's house.
The upper house of the king: most likely the old house of David.
The court of the prison: a prison attached to the king's house, in which were probably put those who offended against the king personally or against his servants and those who worked with him.

The Jews continue repairing the wall from the fountain gate toward the water gate, and Palal repairs opposite the corner at which Binnui, mentioned in the previous verse, ended, and also opposite the tower attached to the upper house of the king and the court of the prison. After Palal, another person called Pedaiah the son of Parosh repaired.

It is noticed that the Holy Bible takes care to mention the name of each one who repaired the wall, to show God's concern for the work of every person who offers Him service, so He records it in His book, as a proclamation that He records every good work and rewards its doer in the Kingdom of Heaven.

Be confident that every good thing you do has value before God, even if others neglect it, despise it or reject it. God thanks you for what you have done and records it with Him so that you may enjoy His reward in eternal life. So continue doing good, whatever the obstacles.

entries.section: (4) The water gate and the horse gate

paragraphs.text: The Nethinim: they are the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua long ago, so he promised not to destroy them, and when he discovered that they dwelt near him, he made them work in the service of the temple, gathering wood and drawing water. Ophel: a part of the hill lying south-east of Jerusalem.

The water gate: the one that leads to the spring of Gihon, which is the main source of fresh water supplying the city of Jerusalem. Opposite the fountain gate there is a large courtyard inside the city in which people gathered either to hear the Holy Scriptures, as Ezra did (Neh 8:1), or in which booths were set up on the days of the Feast of Tabernacles (Neh 8:16). There is an opinion that the water gate is not a gate of the city but a gate of the palace attached to the temple of the Lord. The next group in the repair is the group of the Nethinim, who repaired the wall at the water gate and the outer tower. This shows that all classes of those who worked in the temple took part in repairing the wall, not only the priests and Levites but also the Nethinim; not only the Jews took part but also non-Jews attached to them, for God accepts the service of all and their love, and Christ came for the salvation of all mankind.

The water gate signifies the word of God, which overflows upon everyone who cares for it and satisfies him and works in him and through him. This gate was sound and did not need repair, and it signifies the steadfastness of the word of God.
Do not despise anyone's service, whatever his position, race or religion, for God welcomes and rejoices in all, and He is the One who works in all to draw them to Himself.

entries.section: (4) The water gate and the horse gate

paragraphs.text: The work extended after the water gate toward the east, and the Tekoites repaired a part of the wall. This part is a second section, for after they repaired the first part mentioned in (v. 5) they came forward to repair another part. This shows their activity despite the slackness of their leaders in this work, which did not affect their activity. This new part was opposite the great tower and Ophel.

entries.section: (4) The water gate and the horse gate

paragraphs.text: The horse gate: it lies on the eastern side of the city, north of the water gate, and through it the king's horses entered their stables. It is noticed that the king's palace was near this gate, because the horse gate was near the temple, and beside it were the dwellings of the priests, so they took care to repair it and the wall above it. And because horses take part in war, they represented at that time military strength; therefore the gate of the temple signifies striving and victory.

entries.section: (5) The east gate and the gate Miphkad

paragraphs.text: The east gate: it lies on the eastern side of the city opposite the temple, and it is the first gate opened in the city at sunrise and is considered the main entrance of the temple, and it was later called the Beautiful gate (Acts 3:2). The people continued to take part in repairing the wall: Zadok repaired opposite his house, and after him Shemaiah repaired opposite his house, and Shemaiah was the one responsible for guarding the east gate, for his dwelling was opposite this gate. The east gate signifies the Sun of Righteousness, since it is the first gate from which the sun appears; therefore it signifies the Incarnation of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, who was born in the east, and it also signifies His Second Coming, which will come from the east.

entries.section: (5) The east gate and the gate Miphkad

paragraphs.text: The repair continues after the east gate, moving toward the north. Hananiah and Hanun repaired, and after them Meshullam repaired opposite his house. Perhaps Meshullam was one of the priests and had a position among them, so a chamber was given to him, that is, a dwelling place inside the temple, and he repaired the wall opposite this chamber.

The activity of Hanun is noticed, for he repaired a second section: he first repaired the valley gate (v. 13), and although the Holy Bible mentions that he was the sixth, it most likely means that he was sixth in order among his brothers, not the firstborn or after him. He was filled with more zeal and activity than the rest of his brothers, so he repaired two sections, and it is not mentioned that his brothers repaired anything of the wall, so he may have been the only one who cared for the holy work.

Let no one despise your youth, but be positive and do every good you are able to do, for God is able to work through your weakness greater things than through anyone, so that He is glorified through you and you enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (5) The east gate and the gate Miphkad

paragraphs.text: The house of the Nethinim: most likely a house set up to manage the affairs of the Nethinim in the temple, because the Nethinim lived outside Jerusalem and near it.

The gate Miphkad (the gate of numbering): the armies returning from war entered through it, and the king stood at this gate numbering his returning armies to learn the extent of their victory or defeat before the enemies. This gate lies in the east toward the north and near the king's house, and it is the last of the gates before reaching the sheep gate with which we began.

The work on the wall extends after the east gate as we approach the gate Miphkad, and Malchiah repairs. The Scripture mentions that he was the goldsmith's son, that is, some of the goldsmiths lived east of the city opposite this gate and others lived in the west near the old gate, as we mentioned (v. 8). The merchants also took part in repairing the wall and the gate Miphkad as far as the going up of the turning. As we mentioned, there were many stairs in the city because it is built on hills, and it seems that this stair led to a well-known lane in the city.

The gate Miphkad signifies judgment, because the king stands in person to number his soldiers returning from war, just as the King of kings, our Lord Jesus Christ, will judge the whole world, to separate those victorious over Satan from those who yielded to their lusts.

entries.section: (5) The east gate and the gate Miphkad

paragraphs.text: It is mentioned here that the remaining part of the wall between the going up of the turning and the sheep gate was repaired by the goldsmiths and merchants, in addition to what they had previously repaired in the wall; they used their strength and their money to complete this holy work.

We also notice the concern of some classes, such as the goldsmiths and merchants, for repairing the remaining parts between the repaired sections of the wall, for parts might remain between what the different classes repaired, so they went along the wall to find any parts that had been neglected in order to repair them.

Be a helper to those around you to complete their work and service, even if your name does not appear or you receive no honor from people; but God greatly esteems all your good works and blesses them.
It is noticed that the twelve gates have spiritual meanings, all of which revolve around Christ, as appears in what follows:
1- The sheep gate: signifies Christ, the Lamb incarnate for the redemption of mankind.
2- The fish gate: signifies service and the gathering of souls to faith in Christ.
3- The gate of Ephraim: signifies blessing, since Ephraim was the largest of the tribes in number, for through Christ the Redeemer we have received all blessings.
4- The prison gate: signifies Christ the Redeemer, who freed us from the prison of sin and its bondage and gave us the glorious liberty of the children of God.
5- The old gate: signifies the eternal Christ, everlasting, who is before all worlds, the Ancient of Days, the Creator of all things and the Renewer of our nature.

6- The valley gate: signifies that salvation is within the Church, which Jerusalem signifies, and whoever goes outside Jerusalem falls into the valley of the son of Hinnom, that is, Gehenna. So through Christ the Redeemer inside the Church we obtain salvation by the Holy Sacraments and the means of grace.
7- The dung gate: signifies purity, since the unclean waste is thrown out from it. Through Christ the Redeemer we obtain purity and cleanness in the Holy Sacraments.

8- The fountain gate: signifies the Holy Spirit, who works in us and overflows from us, and through Him we receive new life through the sacrament of Baptism, so that we are born anew in Christ the Savior.
9- The water gate: signifies Christ, the Word of God, who works in His children.
10- The horse gate: signifies spiritual striving and victory over Satan by the power of Christ.
11- The east gate: signifies Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, incarnate for our redemption and coming in His Second Coming to glorify His children.
12- The gate Miphkad: signifies judgment and the recompense of every person according to his works by Christ the Judge.
So we notice that we began with Christ the Redeemer on the Cross and ended with Christ the Judge, for Christ is the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End.

A final note in this chapter: the name of Nehemiah is not mentioned among those who repaired the wall, because he was responsible for directing and organizing the different classes in this work, and this administration is a great work that takes a long time and is harder than the work of repair, since without it the wall would not be completed. For coordinating the work and encouraging it, arranging the defense of the wall against the enemies, and supporting and caring for those taking part in the repair is a work that surpasses all works.
The enemies' opposition to the building of the wall

entries.section: (1) The enemies' mockery and threat of war

paragraphs.text: Sanballat was governor of Samaria on behalf of the Persian kingdom. When he heard the news that the Jews were determined to build a wall around their city Jerusalem, he was greatly angered and enraged at this for the following reasons:

1- The Samaritans believed only in the five books of Moses and offered their worship with images at Bethel and Dan in their land, whereas the Jews believed in all the books of the prophets and offered their worship in the temple at Jerusalem. The building of the wall encourages worship in the temple, and so the deficiency of the Samaritans appears by comparison with those living in Jerusalem and Judea.

2- The Samaritans intermarried with pagan foreigners, which is against the Law of Moses, and this was rejected by the Jews in Jerusalem. Therefore the building of the wall shows the strength of the Jews and their condemnation of what the Samaritans were doing. Sanballat and all those with him were enraged; they were Samaritans, who were originally Jews, but their mingling with the pagans in their worship made him mock the Jews' building of the wall of their city. This shows the extent of his pride, but at the same time it shows his weakness, because he was enraged: he is proud, but inwardly feels weakness before the power of Jerusalem and its temple.

Sanballat's pride made him despise the Jews and not try to stop them by force from building the wall, content to mock them. This was by God's permission, so that Nehemiah might begin building the wall and the Jews be encouraged and not neglect the oppositions of the enemies that would come upon them one after another.

Do not attack others with mockery, thinking it is humor, for this shows how evil your heart is, and your pride and lack of love for others, and even your contempt for them. There is a great difference between gentle humor that makes people happy and condemning others and mocking them, even if they do not answer you out of their politeness and shyness.

entries.section: (1) The enemies' mockery and threat of war

paragraphs.text: His brethren: his senior assistants from the Samaritans in leadership, that is, the chiefs of the people. When Sanballat was enraged, he gathered the chiefs of the people and the commanders of the armies of the Samaritans and began to show his contempt and mockery of the Jews and his confidence in the impossibility of the Jews' being able to build the wall, which appeared in the following:

1- "What do these feeble Jews?" The Assyrian kingdom and then after it the Babylonian kingdom took the best of the Jews to help in the capital of the kingdom and left in Jerusalem and Judea the weak and poor of the people. Therefore Sanballat despised them, declaring with confidence their inability to do a huge work, namely building a wall for Jerusalem, not knowing that the power of God is able to work through the weak.

2- "Will they fortify themselves?" The second reason for the impossibility of building the wall is that the Persian kingdom would not allow the Jews to build this wall, so that all the cities would remain weak and under the control of the Persians.

3- "Will they sacrifice?" With contempt he asserted that they would not be able to complete the wall and then rejoice in it and offer sacrifices to God in thanksgiving and joy at the completion of the work.

4- "Will they make an end in a day?" In view of the hugeness of the wall and its great area, Sanballat showed that it needed a long time, which he imagined would be years, so he said that the zeal of the Jews seemed as if they would complete the wall in a day, and this was impossible in his view.

5- "Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?" The last obstacle is that the Babylonians burned the old wall, so the stones lying around the broken wall are burned and covered with heaps of rubbish, and it is hard to bring them out and renew them to rebuild the wall.

entries.section: (1) The enemies' mockery and threat of war

paragraphs.text: Present at this meeting with Sanballat was Tobiah the Ammonite, who was chief of the children of Ammon, enemies of the Jews who lived beside the Jews to the east of their land. He joined Sanballat in mocking the Jews and added a sixth point confirming the inability of the Jews to build a strong wall for their city. He said that even if the Jews built a wall it would be so weak that a small, light animal like a fox, if it walked on it, would bring it down, and the fox would not need to use its cunning to bring the wall down, because the wall would be so weak that it would fall of itself if the fox walked on it.

entries.section: (1) The enemies' mockery and threat of war

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah did not answer the enemies' mockery but lifted his heart to God in prayer, because it is God who fights for His children and He is their refuge in all their needs. His prayer included the following matters:
1- "We are despised"

He asked God to listen attentively to his prayer, and the people may have joined him in repeating this prayer. And in order to win God's heart he said to Him, we are Your people and Your children, whom the Gentiles mock and reproach, and this of course does not please You because You love Your children.
2- "Turn their reproach upon their own head"

He asked God to turn the mockery of the enemies back upon their own heads if they persisted in their evil, for divine justice demands the punishment of the wicked. This is not a feeling of vengeance or hatred on Nehemiah's part but a showing forth of divine justice, in the hope that through the discipline of the wicked and the success of the righteous all may be led to faith.
3- "Give them for a prey in the land of captivity"

As a discipline from God, Nehemiah asks for the defeat of these enemies in wars, so that they are exposed to the plundering and seizure of their spoils, in the hope that all this may lead them to faith and repentance.
4- "Cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee"

He asks God to continue His discipline of the wicked and not forgive them by blotting out their sins or covering them, but to keep punishing them until they repent; and if they persist in evil, their punishment will be a lesson to others, that they may repent.
5- "For they have provoked thee to anger before the builders"

The sin of the enemies is magnified in that they angered the God of the children of Israel before the Jews who were building the wall, with the intention of bringing a spirit of doubt and despair into them, so that they would stop the work and God would consequently be angry with them.

entries.section: (1) The enemies' mockery and threat of war

paragraphs.text: "All the wall was joined together unto the half thereof": that is, they built the wall around the whole city in a complete circuit but at half the height; so it became a complete wall but still low. Nehemiah and the Jews did not heed the enemies' reproaches but continued to work for God's sake, who is more important than any person, and pleasing Him is above all. Indeed, these reproaches spurred the Jews to zeal in the work so as to show the power of God that supported them and complete the wall in the shortest time, and they built with a heart turned toward God and in unity to accomplish the work.

When Satan fights you, do not be disturbed but resist him, firmly rooted in faith, drive away his thoughts and refuse his lusts, confident that you have authority over him. Continue building your spiritual life and pay no attention to thoughts of doubt and despair, for all of them are from Satan and are not from logic or reality, as he tries to deceive you. For however great your weakness, you are mighty through God who dwells in you.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: The Ashdodites: the inhabitants of Ashdod, one of the five great cities of the Philistines, in which was the temple of the god Dagon, who fell before the ark of the covenant of God in the days of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam 5:3). They were greatly afraid then, but with time they forgot the fear of the God of Israel and allied themselves to fight the Jews. The breaches: the plural of breach, which is a gap inside the wall.

The lands surrounding Jerusalem, when they heard of the building of its wall, were angry, because they feared that Jerusalem would become a power and fight them. So they allied together to fight it, to stop the building of its walls and to kill the workers building the wall. These lands did not have strong relations between one another, but they allied themselves in evil to oppose the city of God.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah was not disturbed but encouraged the rulers and the people, and they prayed to God, and with the help of the rulers he set guards ready for war and for the defense of Jerusalem.

We notice here two things that Nehemiah did: the first is prayer and after it the guarding of Jerusalem. He began with prayer because God is the Giver of strength, and then he did his duty, which was guarding the city.

In all your problems and projects, indeed in all your works, begin with prayer, and at the same time do not be lax in carrying out your duty with all exactness. However great your weakness, God will complete you and make you succeed.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: A new opposition began after the three previous oppositions, which are:
1- Accusing the Jews of rebelling against the state (2:19).
2- Mocking them and despising them (ch. 4:1).
3- Plotting a war to stop the building of the wall and to harm Jerusalem (ch. 4:8).

4- And this opposition is the one found in this verse, and it came from the Jews themselves, from the tribe of Judah, that is, those living in Jerusalem and Judea, for they declared that the work was huge and that the rubbish they carried, which lay around the wall, was very great, and the carriers no longer had strength to continue the work of removing this rubbish. These voices were from Jews who were informants for the enemies, spreading a spirit of doubt and weakness among those working in the building, as they declared their inability to continue the work and spread this among the people. Thus two oppositions joined together, namely the war plotted by the enemies with the spirit of doubt and the weakening of the resolve of those working on the wall.

Do not be disturbed if the wicked gather against you and afflictions multiply, for they are worthless before the power of God that is in you. Seek God and persevere in your striving, and be faithful in your work, confident in the power of God, which overcomes those who oppose you.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: The enemies plotted a military plan for a sudden attack on Jerusalem, so that the enemies would infiltrate and the Jews would be surprised by the war launched against them with the enemies in their midst fighting them.

But God's grace supported Nehemiah, and the secret news of the war plotted against them reached him. Most likely it came from Jews living beside the enemies, who were faithful to their city and did not fear the enemies, and they informed Nehemiah of what was being plotted against Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: From all places whence ye shall return unto us: all the lands outside Jerusalem in which Jews dwell beside the enemies, and from which they returned to their holy city Jerusalem, whether to take part in building the wall or only to report this military plot.

Many of the Jews living outside Jerusalem and those working on the building of the wall confirmed the news of this plotted war, and they informed Nehemiah ten times, that is, many times, of this plotted war.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: Their bows: the plural of bow, which is used for shooting arrows.

Nehemiah organized the guarding of the wall and the city. He stationed guards behind the parts of the wall whose building was not complete, that is, where the wall was still low, and then in the places where the wall had risen and was complete he stationed guards, referred to as the higher places of the wall. Thus he arranged a guard around the whole city and was not disturbed that the wall was incomplete.

The organization of the guard was with wisdom on Nehemiah's part, for the guards stood according to their clans, each clan guarding a certain part, so that cooperation among them would be easy because of their kinship to one another.

Most likely he stationed archers with bows on the high places, and in the low places, that is, on the ground behind the low wall, the men carried swords and spears. He was confident in the power of God that was with them. For though the enemies were trained men of war and the Jews were weak and untrained in war, Nehemiah made every possible preparation and relied on God, the Guardian of his city.

entries.section: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah took care to encourage the rulers and the people who were ready for war, declaring the invincible supporting power of God. For Nehemiah is a popular leader who takes care to persuade everyone to defend their city bravely and in faith, and he is a thoughtful leader who looks at and investigates the matter and then rises to plan and distribute the work and encourage the workers to guard the city. Nehemiah took care to stir up the zeal and jealousy of the people to defend their city, because in it were their wives, their children and their homes, since they would not accept being taken captive or killed by the enemies.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: Sanballat and Tobiah and all their followers among the enemies learned that their plots for a sudden invasion of Jerusalem had been discovered by the people of God, who had prepared for them and did not fear their power. So their plots failed and the people of God returned, each one to his work on the wall; that is, they were not held back by these threats, but the people of God felt His power supporting them and bringing the plots of the enemies to nothing, so they rejoiced and were firm in their faith.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: Spears: the plural of spear, which is a metal rod pointed at its end, a weapon of war for stabbing the enemy.

Shields: the plural of shield, which is a piece of wood covered with leather with a handle at the back, into which the soldier puts his hand and moves the shield in front of his face and body to protect him from arrows.
Habergeons: the plural of habergeon, which is metal clothing covering the chest and stomach to protect the soldier from arrows and spears or any weapon of war.
With wisdom Nehemiah divided those working with him into two parts: the first part built the wall, and the second part bore arms to guard the wall from the attacks of the enemies.
And they carried the various weapons used in war at that time:

The rulers did their work of encouraging those who built the wall or those who guarded it, so that they would accomplish their works for God's sake. A part of the workers devoted themselves to bearing arms, which had two benefits: the guarding of the wall, and also a rest for the guards from the toil of building, so that they might regain their strength and then return to the hard work of building, which some had begun to tire of because of the great amount of rubbish they were carrying (v. 10).

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: The meaning of this is that half of the men worked on building the wall, whether in laying stones or carrying earth, and the other half guarded the wall. To express this it says that with one hand they built and with the other they held a weapon, that is, half of them built and the other half guarded. It does not of course mean that he carried a load with one hand and held a weapon in the other hand, for that is not practical.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: Besides dividing the workers into a part for guarding and a part for building, the workers also each carried his sword on his thigh, and most likely it was a small sword that did not hinder the worker's movement in building, whereas the one responsible for guarding carried the various weapons mentioned before in v. 16. Nehemiah himself inspected the work on the wall and encouraged the builders and the guards, and beside him was a man carrying a large trumpet which, when he blew it, everyone in Jerusalem would hear its sound, in order to direct them and gather them when needed for war.

It is good in your spiritual striving to take care to guard your senses and thoughts and keep them away from every sin, and at the same time to take care of positive work such as prayers, readings and services, for the two complete each other for your spiritual growth.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah agreed with the rulers who helped him in managing the city and with all the chiefs that they should teach the people working on building the wall, and the guards, that because of the wide extent of the wall it was hard for them to hear one another; therefore when they heard the trumpet they should gather to it, because Nehemiah and the trumpeter would remain at the place from which the enemies attacked, and by the blowing of the trumpet they would gather the people to the same place to repel the enemies' attack.
And this confirms many things, which are:
1- That Nehemiah was inspecting and watching the work and the areas surrounding Jerusalem, that is, following the building and the preparation for the enemies' attacks.

2- Although they bore arms everywhere on the wall to guard it, at the attack they gather with one heart, and God looks upon their love and their attachment to Him and to one another, and so He intervenes and fights the enemies for them. They gather to declare their unity, their submission to God and their faith in His power defending them.
3- The trumpet signifies the word of God, which gathers the faithful into one mind, the mind of Christ, and He fights for them against the attacks of Satan.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: The earnestness in the work is noticed here, from the break of dawn until full darkness when the stars appear, and therefore the guard too was complete from dawn to night.

Seize the opportunity of life to work faithfully. This life is signified by the day, as Christ says, "Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you" (Jn 12:35). So as long as you are able to worship God and serve Him, and to be faithful in every work for His sake, you must work before the darkness comes, that is, death.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah also took care to guard Jerusalem and its wall all night long, so he made some of the men lodge with their helpers in the midst of Jerusalem and inside its walls; that is, not all lodged in their homes, but he organized a night guard as he organized the day guard.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah and his relatives, helpers and guards were an example to the rest of the men in activity all day long, for they did not take off their clothes and their weapons, in order to continue the work however long the day. The only exception to taking off the clothes was when they went to the water to wash and bathe.
Nehemiah cares for the needy

1- If the previous chapter tells us about the external enemies who stood against the people of God to prevent them from building the wall, this chapter tells us about the internal troubles among the people of God, such as injustice and the exploitation of the weak.

2- The events of this chapter did not happen during the building of the wall, but began a long time earlier, either in the days of Nehemiah or before his governorship over Jerusalem. Then the poor presented their complaints near the end of the period of Nehemiah's governorship, which lasted twelve years, as is shown by what is mentioned in (v. 14). This is because the troubles of the poor had increased, and on the other hand they found in Nehemiah the good and just governor who could do them justice and have compassion on them.

entries.section: (1) The complaint of the poor

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah met a great problem among the people of God, for the poor came forward with a complaint, crying out to God and to the governor Nehemiah against the exploitation of them by the rich Jews during the economic hardships they were passing through. They were barely getting the necessary food, or less than it, and suffered from the problems of humiliation and bondage.

It is noticed that most of the Jews were poor and faced this suffering, as shown by their saying "the cry of the people," and from the severity of their misery the women went out with their husbands, so that Nehemiah would lift the injustice from them and help them to live.

entries.section: (1) The complaint of the poor

paragraphs.text: The complaint of the poor contained the following:
1- The large number of sons and daughters in poor families, and this was customary and still is to this day.
2- Their great need for the necessary food, which is bread, so they declared that they had no wheat.

entries.section: (1) The complaint of the poor

paragraphs.text: It is clear from this verse that Judea was suffering from hunger, and this was due either to the scarcity of rain or to the people's neglect of farming during the building of the wall.
The poor people were forced to give their fields, the inheritance of their fathers, in pledge to their rich brethren in order to obtain their necessary food, which was wheat.

These rich among the Jews had either brought money from Babylon and its surroundings, where they had lived before their return from the captivity, or had special activity and abilities that qualified them to set up projects and succeed in them, so they obtained much money.

The rich took their brethren's fields in pledge in order to give them the necessary food, and this was contrary to the Law, because the Law forbids exploiting the poor and seizing their possessions (Deut 24:10-13); that is, a pledge is acceptable if it is for setting up projects and not for necessary needs.

entries.section: (1) The complaint of the poor

paragraphs.text: The king's tribute: taxes collected by the empire from all the peoples subject to it, so that they pay a tax on every person.

The poor people also suffered from their inability to pay the king's tribute, and they were forced to borrow from their rich brethren to pay the tribute, and these loans carried usury. This is contrary to the Law, as we said, because usury is permitted in dealings between the rich with one another, but as for the poor, the Law provides that usury is not to be taken from them (Ex 22:25, Mt 25:27).

entries.section: (1) The complaint of the poor

paragraphs.text: The complaint of the poor also included their being forced to sell their daughters as maidservants to their rich brethren. This was very painful to their souls, because they were unable to free their daughters so that they might live with them in their homes a dignified life.
The complaint was severe, for the poor said that they were circumcised in their flesh like their brethren, so why should they be enslaved to them.

The strange thing is that the rich among the Jews forgot that a short time earlier they had all been enslaved to Babylon, and before it to Assyria. But when their circumstances became easier and they obtained some money, they seized the opportunity of their brethren's poverty and enslaved them in selfishness.
May you be merciful to those around you and feel their material and psychological needs, so that you obtain God's mercies on earth, and after that in heaven.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah listened attentively to the people's complaint, which came from suffering hearts, and was not distracted from them by his concern for building the wall or by repelling the plots of the enemies. This shows Nehemiah's fatherhood and his justice as a responsible governor.

This anger of Nehemiah, the responsible one, declares the uprightness of his heart and his rejection of sin, and on the other hand reassures the wronged that he cared for them and would not neglect their demands. At the same time this anger shows Nehemiah's impartiality toward the rich: he wants nothing from anyone, and he is strong, declaring the truth even if he angers some people, even if they are among the great of the people, for he fears God and therefore fears no one. This is the first step Nehemiah took, namely his anger at sin.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: The second step Nehemiah took was consulting with himself. His anger was not impulsive, but he thought wisely how the just and fitting course of action should be.

The third step: with courage he rebuked the rich and the rulers of the people for exploiting the poor and for their silence about the injustice, because they took usury when they lent to the poor, although they knew of their inability to pay for the necessities of life.

The fourth step: he set a great assembly against the exploiting great men, namely a large number of the poor people as representatives of the rest of the people; that is, he confronted the rich with what they had done to these poor, and the truth became clear, which was injustice and severe exploitation. He is just, hearing both points of view, the complainant and the one complained against, to be sure of the soundness of the case.

By these actions and what follows in the next verses Nehemiah's distinction from Ezra in the internal reform of the people appears. Ezra wept and tore his garments, declaring his distress at the evil (Ezra 9:3-5), but Nehemiah added strong steps in the reform, for he rebuked the wrongdoers and did good things, as will appear in the rest of the chapter.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah said in his rebuke of the great men that many of the Jews had been enslaved to the Gentiles, and Nehemiah and other godly men had been able to free as many as possible of the enslaved Jews. Nehemiah wonders at the great men, that after their brethren were freed they go back and enslave them. So the great men were silent in shame and in acknowledgment of their sin.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah showed them their sin in exploiting their poor brethren, and that this conduct of theirs was evil and angered God, and by this sin of theirs they declared their lack of fear of God and their treating evil as permissible.

On the other hand, they increase the Gentiles' reproach against them, since they are poor and humiliated, and therefore this declares the inability of their God to provide for them and give them a dignified life, and by this the rich insult God. Then the Gentiles find a clear sin in the people of God, namely their cruelty and their wronging one another; that is, that the Law of God cannot spread justice among His people.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: The fifth step Nehemiah took in solving this problem was a positive action by him and those working with him in managing the affairs of Jerusalem, for they came forward to help the poor with money that they lent them to meet their needs, so that they would not need to borrow from the rich usurers who exploited them. At the end of the verse, as a sixth step, he demands of the rich that they leave off usury, that is, when they recover their money from the poor they do not take more than what they lent.

And out of Nehemiah's humility he says "let us leave off this usury," to encourage the rich to do so. He did not say to them "leave off," but "let us leave off," and this was great gentleness on his part.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich
