paragraphs.text: The seventh step Nehemiah took was his command to the great men and the rulers to restore at once the fields and houses they had taken in pledge from the poor, and by this they would have an opportunity to find food and live a dignified life.

He also demanded that they restore the usury they had taken, the amount of which was the hundredth part, that is, 1% monthly, and this means that they were taking 12% a year as interest on their loans to the poor.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: The great men obeyed Nehemiah and restored the property and money to the poor, and this shows the extent of Nehemiah's awe and authority, so that the great men feared him, for they saw in him the Spirit of God and justice.

The eighth step was Nehemiah's appointing the priests as responsible for carrying out what the rich had promised, considering the priests as knowing the Law and responsible for carrying it out, to warn every one who fell short or was slack in it. By this Nehemiah confirmed the promise of the rich, and it became a covenant between them and God, whom the priests represent.

entries.section: (2) The rebuke of the rich

paragraphs.text: I shook my lap: shaking the lap was an ancient custom meaning the cursing of the other person. They used to make a pocket in the garment in which they put leaves or anything similar, and they shook it out when needed to declare their curse and anger on whoever stood before them.

The ninth and last step Nehemiah took was shaking out his lap before the great men, declaring that curses would come upon everyone who did not carry out what he had commanded, that is, he would be cursed by God, deprived of every blessing, and God would shake out every person who did not do this, that is, forsake him and drive him far away and empty his house of blessing, because he had not put out of his house and his possessions the money of injustice that he had taken from the poor. The great men agreed to Nehemiah's words, saying "Amen," as the people did long ago in the days of Moses at the mountains of Gerizim and Ebal, when they heard the blessings and the curses that would come upon them for obeying God's commandments or rejecting them.

After this the great men prayed and praised God and glorified Him because He had turned them back from sin so that they might live by His commandments, and they carried out all that God commanded through the mouth of Nehemiah, and were saved from falling into division between the rich and the poor and the revolts that result from it.

If you are responsible in any place, do not be lax with sin, and declare your anger at it, so that everyone around you turns back from it. Declaring the truth is your first responsibility, so that you are the first to keep the word of God.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah, an example of self-giving

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah became governor of Judea by the command of King Artaxerxes, when he declared to him his concern to build a wall for Jerusalem. He remained governor for twelve years.

During this period Nehemiah was an example of sacrifice, for he did not use his natural right to obtain his material needs of food and drink, for himself and his brethren, or his helpers in administering the province, or his relatives, but gave up this right. He took no taxes from the people to provide for his needs, but it seems that he relied on his own money, which he had obtained when he worked as cupbearer to the king in the capital Shushan the palace, before he became governor of Jerusalem and Judea.
Nehemiah's giving up his natural right shows the following:
1- That he is an example in giving and in feeling for the poor, so that the rich would imitate him, and he did not of course intend boasting. The rest of the chapter shows his noble purpose.

2- Since he gave up his right, he is not biased in his command, but gave a lesson to the great men to keep the Law and have compassion on their poor brethren, for he does not want to take anything of the money of the rich for himself.

May you learn self-giving from Nehemiah if you are responsible in your home, or your work, or a servant in the Church, so that you prefer the comfort of others and give up your own comfort and material needs, and put others before yourself.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah, an example of self-giving

paragraphs.text: A shekel of silver: equal to 11.6 grams (the shekel of the sanctuary). The governors who preceded Nehemiah in governing Jerusalem and Judea were accustomed to take from the people the needs of the governor's palace of food and drink, in addition to forty shekels of silver, equal to about 464 grams, that is, about half a kilogram of silver, and this was most likely given daily to the governor's palace. They paid no heed to the poverty and weakness of the people but looked to their own comfort.
These governors are not meant to be Ezra or Zerubbabel, but the governors who were foreign to the Jews, whom the empire appointed.

We see Nehemiah's love and his keeping away from error in not condemning a certain person, in that he did not mention the names of these governors. He does not intend to condemn anyone, but to make clear the idea of self-giving that Nehemiah practices, and he calls the great men to follow it.
The burdening of the people was in three things, which are:
1- Demanding the governor's bread.
2- Taking forty shekels.
3- The governor's helpers exploited the people and obtained money and possessions from them.

Because Nehemiah feared God, he refused to exploit the people, or even to obtain only his personal needs from them, because he had compassion on them. By this he is an example for the great men to fear God and not exploit the poor.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah, an example of self-giving

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah's goodness as governor appears in the following:
1- His first concern was the completion of his work, which was building the wall, and not his personal comfort as governor.
2- He did not care to own fields or any possessions, but on the contrary used his personal money to help the poor of the people.

3- Because Nehemiah was concerned to stand in person to oversee the work of building the wall and its gates, his helpers also moved to manage the building work in imitation of him, and did not seek their own comfort by exploiting the people. From this appears the difference between Nehemiah's servants, that is, his helpers, and the servants of the former governors, who exploited the people.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah, an example of self-giving

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah used to host in the governor's palace more than a hundred and fifty men, who were:
1- The Jews who came with him from Babylon.
2- The Jewish rulers responsible for the cities subject to him.
3- The Gentile rulers governing the cities subject to him.
4- The guests from the Gentile nations surrounding Judea, who visited the governor.

Nehemiah spent on these daily tables from his personal salary, which he obtained as the king's governor, in addition to his money that he had and had saved when he was the king's cupbearer, but he did not exploit the people to obtain money.

Nehemiah here is a type of Christ, who offered His table, that is, the altar of the Church of the New Testament, to Christians of Jewish or Gentile origin. He offered on His table the greatest food, which is His most holy Body and Blood, as Nehemiah offered the greatest foods and wines he could.

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah, an example of self-giving

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah shows us the hugeness of the tables in his palace: they required the slaughter of an ox daily, in addition to six choice sheep, and likewise a large number of birds, the number of which is not mentioned because of their abundance. He also offered the different kinds of wines at greater tables held every ten days in the governor's palace.

All this was at Nehemiah's personal expense, because his tender heart had compassion on the poor people, who suffered from the cruelty of bondage to the empire, for they paid it heavy taxes despite the weakness of their resources, as appears in (v. 4). From these tables we understand that Nehemiah was distinguished by the virtue of clearly welcoming strangers, as Abraham, the father of fathers, did (Gen 18).

entries.section: (3) Nehemiah, an example of self-giving

paragraphs.text: In all that Nehemiah did of self-giving and sacrifices we see the following meanings:
1- He offers all his good works to God, and does not intend by them any special honor or praise from anyone.
2- In humility he declares his need to God, that he needs God's goodness and care for him.

3- In self-emptying of his own will he did not specify particular requests from God, that is, the kind of good he wanted from God, but left that to God to choose for him the good that suits him, for he trusts in God and so does not ask for personal desires.
The completion of the wall despite the plots. The enemies of Nehemiah, who signify the demons, tried to stop the building of the wall, which signifies the building of our spiritual life, by means of:
1- External threats and wars (chs. 2, 4).
2- Internal wars of problems among the people of God (ch. 5).
3- Wars directed at the leader Nehemiah to get rid of him, so that the building would stop (ch. 6).

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: The enemies of Nehemiah heard that he had been able to build the whole wall and that no breach remained in it, that is, it had become complete, and nothing remained but for him to make the gates of the city and set up their doors (leaves). They were greatly distressed and felt that their four previous plots had failed, which are mentioned in (chs. 2, 4), and they are:
1- Accusing the Jews of rebelling against the empire (ch. 2:19).
2- Mocking the Jews and despising the wall that they were building (ch. 4:1).
3- Plotting a war to attack Jerusalem and thereby hinder the building of the wall (ch. 4:8).
4- Weakening the resolve of the Jewish builders by sending Jews who were informants for the enemies (ch. 4:10).

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: The plain of Ono: a village in the tribe of Benjamin, lying on the border of the tribe of Benjamin and the land of Samaria, north of Jerusalem at a distance of 32 km.

Two of Nehemiah's enemies, Sanballat and Geshem, sent to Nehemiah asking him to come to the plain of Ono to negotiate with him, saying that there were accusations directed against him and they did not want these accusations to reach the king. In truth they intended to kill Nehemiah on the way, or to seize him in the village of Ono. The deceit of the enemies appears in the fact that the village of Ono has no walls, so that Nehemiah would be reassured that they did not want to detain him in a walled city, whereas in truth they did not want to negotiate but to seize him or kill him. And if they could not, they would at least hinder the building of the wall, even if only for a few days, the days of negotiation.

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: Negotiating with the wicked is of no benefit, but harmful. This is what Eve fell into when she negotiated and conversed with the serpent, and fell. Therefore we see Nehemiah refusing to negotiate, occupied with the positive work, which was building the wall.

And we find Nehemiah saying, "I am doing a great work," which shows his sense of responsibility for the work and his absorption in it so as to complete it for God's sake; that is, with all his heart he is bound to the service of God. Although Nehemiah understood the evil plan of his enemies, which was an attempt to kill him or seize him, he gave a logical reason for refusing to negotiate, namely his being occupied with building the wall, which would be hindered if he left it to negotiate with them.

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: When Nehemiah refused to negotiate with the enemies, they repeated their request; that is, they invited him four times to negotiate, but he kept refusing, for he was firm in holding to the positive work. Of course their insistence shows their evil, just as Satan presses us to commit sin.

The evil of the enemies is clear, because if they had been sincere in their love they would have come to him in Jerusalem. Nehemiah's holding fast to staying in Jerusalem, which is the holy place and signifies the strong fortress, was good. Nehemiah offered nothing in answer to the enemies' request but the excuse of being occupied in building the wall; he was occupied in the service of God, and did not speak of the evil of the enemies, so as not to waste his time in foolish arguments.

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: Sanballat sent a fifth message and invitation to Nehemiah to negotiate. At this stage the invitation was not an oral message but a written letter. Letters in ancient times were written on parchment, that is, thin skin, and sometimes on papyrus, and were delivered as follows:
1- Either they were rolled up and sealed and put inside a box, to be kept secret and out of respect for the person to whom it was sent.
2- Or they were not sealed and not put in a box, so that anyone could read them before they reached their owner. Sanballat sent the letter in the second way, and this means two things.
a- Contempt for Nehemiah, because the sealing of a letter means the greatness of the one to whom it is sent.
b- So that the people would read it before it reached Nehemiah, and doubt and fear and press Nehemiah to negotiate with Sanballat, and so the work would stop.
By this method Sanballat intended to disturb Nehemiah so that he would do one of these things:
1- Fear and the abandonment of building the wall.
2- Fear and hastening to negotiate with Sanballat, because the letter contained the accusation of Nehemiah that he wanted to set himself up as king and rebel against the king of Persia.
3- Traveling to the king to declare his innocence, so that the work would stop.

4- Accusing the people of taking part in the rebellion, so that they would fear and not help Nehemiah in building the wall. Sanballat accused Nehemiah of having appointed prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim him king in Jerusalem, to make it and Judea independent of the king of Persia. This accusation was based on the fact that Malachi in the third chapter of his prophecy spoke of the awaited Messiah. So Sanballat accused Nehemiah of having appointed this Malachi and others to help in setting him up as king, since the Messiah in Sanballat's view was Nehemiah.

Sanballat claimed that the Gentile nations around the Jews were saying that Nehemiah wanted to set himself up as king, and that Geshem the Arabian, one of Nehemiah's enemies and one of the great and well-known figures, had heard this talk and told Sanballat of it. And Sanballat comes forward to Nehemiah as a friend to negotiate with him, to protect him from these reports. All this was a lie and pretense on Sanballat's part, to frighten Nehemiah and hinder the building.

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: In faith in God Nehemiah answered Sanballat that his words were a lie and an untrue pretense. Nehemiah's answer was in these brief words because he was occupied with his aim, which was building the wall, so as to complete it as soon as possible.

entries.section: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: The threats and fears sent to Nehemiah increased, along with false claims that the Jews were afraid and that their interest and strength in the building were weak, but he was not shaken, and did two important things:
1- He prayed to God and asked for His help and strengthening.
2- He made a vow to God to complete the work, and here Nehemiah's determination to complete the building is understood implicitly, and he asks God to strengthen him.
Hold fast to your spiritual striving and every building work you do, and rely on prayer. Then you will not be disturbed by Satan's hindrances that try to trouble you and take you away from God.

entries.section: (2) The false prophets frighten Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: After the failure of the fifth attempt to stop the building of the wall, which was luring Nehemiah to negotiate with Sanballat, mentioned in (vv. 1-9), the enemies plotted the sixth and last plot to hinder the building, but God exposed it to Nehemiah and helped him until he completed the wall.

The sixth plot was extremely dangerous, for it was a carefully planned scheme. Shemaiah invited Nehemiah to visit him in his house. This Shemaiah was considered a great prophet in Israel, and it seems that he spent many periods in seclusion in his house, as shown by his saying that his house was shut up. Because of Shemaiah's standing, Nehemiah went to him to listen to his counsel and wisdom, which were known in Israel. Shemaiah said to him, showing friendship and concern for him, that Tobiah and the rest of the enemies were trying to kill him, and this was clear from the previous plots. He suggested to him a way to escape from their hand: that he go with him to the temple and hide there and they shut the doors on themselves, so that the enemies could not reach Nehemiah, because the temple had doorkeepers and guards, in addition to its being forbidden to any non-Jew to enter the temple. Then Shemaiah's suggestion was to enter into the midst of the temple, meaning by this the Holy Place, where only the priests enter, so the enemies could not reach him. It appears from Shemaiah's words that he was telling him of a specific plot that he had learned of, either by divine counsel or through his contact with the people, who considered him and honored him, so they could convey news to him.

Shemaiah's plot appears to be carefully planned, since Shemaiah was in his shut-up house to suggest to Nehemiah that he was in seclusion, so divine revelations might be expected to have reached him. And Shemaiah's specifying the time of the enemies' attempt to kill Nehemiah, namely at night, confirms to Nehemiah that it is a divine revelation.
And Shemaiah's summoning Nehemiah to his shut-up house suggests to Nehemiah that the words are secret and serious, in addition to their being a divine revelation, as we said.

Shemaiah exploited in these words Nehemiah's love for God, and therefore his taking refuge in the temple would be a thing dear to him. But this plot had a flaw, which is that it was not right for Nehemiah to enter the midst of the temple, because he was not a priest, and his entering would be against the Law of God.

entries.section: (2) The false prophets frighten Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: God revealed to Nehemiah the plot of Shemaiah, and most likely Nehemiah had lifted up a prayer to God, who guided him how to act. He rejected Shemaiah's suggestion for the following reasons:

1- His submitting to Shemaiah's suggestion would declare that he was afraid of the enemies, and this conflicts with faith, so God would be displeased with him and he would lose His protection and care.

2- Nehemiah's hiding and fear would make fear creep into the hearts of his people, so they too would flee and leave off completing the wall, that is, making the gates, which would expose Jerusalem to the enemies' attack.

3- Nehemiah's entering the midst of the temple, that is, the Holy Place, which no one is allowed to enter except the priests, would greatly provoke God against him, in addition to provoking the anger of the priests against him, because they held fast to the Law, and by this division would occur, and this would stop the completion of the wall.

4- Nehemiah is a responsible person who wants to complete the wall whatever the cost, even if it were his life. He is ready to complete the work even if he died for the sake of God and his people, and in this he is a type of Christ the Redeemer.

entries.section: (2) The false prophets frighten Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: When Nehemiah obeyed the voice of God, which he sensed after prayer, and in faith rejected Shemaiah's counsel, ready to face death for his people, God revealed to him the plot of Shemaiah, and he became sure that his words were at the instigation of the enemies Tobiah and Sanballat, who had hired him for this base work against God and his people, and against Nehemiah the great leader, most likely in return for material gifts. Shemaiah here is a type of Judas Iscariot the traitor, who betrayed Christ his Teacher, whom Nehemiah signifies.

entries.section: (2) The false prophets frighten Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: The enemies' purpose in Shemaiah's plot was to make Nehemiah fall into sin, so that he would abandon God, and then the disgrace of sin would come upon him, and he would lose his standing as leader of the people and become despised, and therefore be unable to lead his people in the spiritual way and in building Jerusalem and raising it up.

entries.section: (2) The false prophets frighten Nehemiah

paragraphs.text: From this plot we discover that Nehemiah faced a severe war from the enemies by means of a group of false prophets in Jerusalem and Judea, headed by Shemaiah and Noadiah the prophetess, two false prophets who are not mentioned in the Holy Bible except here.

These prophets tried in various ways and with false prophecies to frighten Nehemiah, and they were all hired by the enemies Tobiah and Sanballat, but he held fast to God and so was able to stand firm in faith and overcome their plots.

This plot shows the enemies' insistence on fighting Nehemiah to the last moment to stop the completion of the wall, as Satan does, who keeps fighting the children of God all their lives. It is noticed that Nehemiah's heart was not filled with evil toward the enemies, but he left the matter to God to act as He saw fit to do toward these wicked men. He is a man occupied with the positive work and has no spirit of revenge toward those who are hostile to him.

Believe in God who loves you and trust in His ability to protect you. Even in the midst of dangers lift your heart in prayer to Him in every situation, confident that He is near you and will guide you to what is for your good.

entries.section: (3) The completion of the wall and Tobiah's relations

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah completed the building of the wall and its gates in fifty-two days, taking into account that they rested on the Sabbath day. It is clear that the building of the wall was done in a very short time for the following reasons:
1- The help of God, who crowns the striving of His children with great support.
2- The concern of all the people to take part in building the wall, so the number of workers was very great.
3- The order and arrangement with which the building was done, for each group was responsible for repairing a specific part of the wall, that is, responsibility was assigned to each group.
4- The wall was not all broken down but only parts of it, in addition to the fallen stones lying on the ground beside the wall, which the workers took and completed the building with.
5- Nehemiah's and his helpers' encouragement of the people, and his leading the work himself.

The building was completed on the twenty-fifth of the month of Elul in the year 444 B.C., and this month corresponds to the month of September in the Gregorian year. Daniel had prophesied in the year 605 B.C. the completion of the building of the wall (Dan 9:25).

entries.section: (3) The completion of the wall and Tobiah's relations

paragraphs.text: When Nehemiah's enemies learned that he had completed the building of the wall, they felt the following:
1- They were ashamed and abashed and felt their weakness, since all their attempts to stop the building had failed.

2- They envied the Jews, who were able to fortify their city Jerusalem, while the enemies' cities were not fortified like it, and they had not been able to obtain permission for this from the emperor.

3- They were sure that this great success was by the power of God, and therefore could not be resisted; that is why all their attempts failed. But sadly they did not believe in God or fear Him, and their wars against the people of God were repeated afterward.

entries.section: (3) The completion of the wall and Tobiah's relations

paragraphs.text: After the failure of Tobiah, the greatest enemy of the Jews, and the completion of the building of the wall, Tobiah did not surrender but kept fighting the people of God with cunning and malice by means of:
1- Relations with the chiefs of the tribe of Judah, and even an alliance with them, and perhaps this was through gifts that Tobiah gave to the chiefs, as shown by their testimony to him in (v. 19).

2- The intermarriage of the Jews with foreign women of the Gentiles, from the sons and daughters of Tobiah and Sanballat, so the sons of Tobiah married the children of the chiefs of Judah, Shechaniah and Meshullam. By this intermarriage Tobiah was able to learn the news of the Jews, and even to spread among them whatever news he wanted in order to influence them and weaken them.
3- The passing of many letters from the chiefs of Judah to Tobiah and the reverse, which made Tobiah know the news of the Jews and influence them also.

4- By Tobiah's relations he influenced many of the chiefs of Judah, so they began to praise Tobiah before Nehemiah as a generous and great man who loved the Jews, although he was deceitful and established these relations for his own benefit and gave gifts to deceive and win the chiefs of Judah.
5- When the attempts to praise Tobiah before Nehemiah failed, Tobiah began to send reports to frighten Nehemiah, to make him lose his ability to lead and be shaken before his people.

Do not be disturbed by the continuing wars of Satan, for they are worthless before the power of God that is in you, and do not be disturbed either by the deception of many of the loved ones around you by the ideas of the world, but be steadfast in God's commandments and all you learned in the Church, confident that God who is in you is stronger than all the power of the demons, your enemies. The guarding of Jerusalem and the genealogies of the people. After Nehemiah's success in building the wall he was encouraged to enter into other positive works, so he took care to guard the city, and then took care also of the people living in Jerusalem, so he searched out their genealogies, especially of the priests and Levites, to care for the service of the temple and to establish the people spiritually with God. So after Nehemiah's success in the external work, which was the wall, he took care of the internal work, which was the guarding of the city and the spiritual life of its inhabitants. For whoever begins to work gains the positive spirit in all his life. Chapters 1-6 speak about the building of the wall, and from chapter 7 to the end of the book they tell us about the building of the people.

entries.section: (1) The guarding of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: After the wall of Jerusalem and its gates were completed, Nehemiah turned his attention to the service of the Temple. He appointed gatekeepers to guard the gates of the Temple, and also singers to chant the Psalms, as David had arranged in former times. After that he also appointed Levites to help the priests and to carry out all the work of the Temple.

entries.section: (1) The guarding of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: After arranging the service of the Temple, Nehemiah began to give his attention to organizing the city of Jerusalem. He set two rulers over it. The first was Hanani, who was mentioned in (ch. 1:2) and whom Nehemiah describes as “my brother.” He was a man concerned for Jerusalem; during the captivity he used to visit it in order to look into its condition, as is clear in (ch. 1), and he also came with Nehemiah to take part in building the wall. He was a responsible man who could be relied upon, and a lover of Jerusalem, the city of God. The word “brother” means either that he was his brother according to the flesh, or that he was one of his relatives.

The other man whom Nehemiah chose to govern Jerusalem was Hananiah, whom he had tested in the command of the royal palace, and whose faithfulness and ability in administration had been shown. So he entrusted all of Jerusalem to him together with Hanani.

For God sets over much the one who is faithful in little. Hananiah was also distinguished by his fear of God, which made him careful and far from evil, and therefore Nehemiah could be at ease in entrusting the government of Jerusalem to him.

This shows Nehemiah's excellence in administration: he placed officials in every place while he himself supervised them all. The distribution of responsibilities is necessary for successful administration; moreover, if the supreme leader, Nehemiah, is absent, affairs still go on, because there is an official in every place. This is what happened when Nehemiah traveled to the capital of the empire and then returned to Jerusalem a second time, as is mentioned in (ch. 13).

Do not hold all matters in your own hand in order to please yourself, or because you doubt everyone around you. Rather, you should take care to distribute responsibilities, to encourage those who are responsible, to follow up on them, and to accept their weaknesses and make up for them. Then you will be a successful administrator and will please God.

entries.section: (1) The guarding of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, gave the following orders to the administrative officials Hanani and Hananiah:
1- That they should see for themselves that the gates of the city were shut every evening.

2- That the gates should not be opened at dawn, as was formerly customary, but at sunrise. The purpose was that the few inhabitants of Jerusalem should have awakened and even left their houses, and movement should have begun in the city; only then would visitors and merchants enter. Thus the enemy would not seize the chance to attack the city at dawn while many were still asleep.

3- That each one should guard the wall opposite his own house. That is, the guard over the wall, or behind the gates, was to be organized among the inhabitants of Jerusalem by turns, so that one man from each house would go out to keep watch. This was for the following reasons:

a - The number of the inhabitants of Jerusalem was still small, and new houses had not yet been built after the destruction of Jerusalem at the hands of Babylon. There were only a few old houses, in which of course only a small number of people lived.

b - The guarding of the wall opposite its own house by each family confirms the sense of responsibility and of belonging to Jerusalem; each one defends his own house with care, and so the work of guarding the whole city is made complete.

The distribution of the watch among the inhabitants did not remove the responsibility of Hanani and Hananiah, for they supervised the watch so that, if they found any negligence, they would speak to the one concerned and warn the negligent. This signifies that each person is responsible for the salvation of his own soul, yet the priests and servants warn everyone who draws away from God.

The population of Jerusalem was small, perhaps because the city was in ruins and did not encourage settlement, except for those who cared to dwell near the Temple. In addition, of the fifty thousand who returned with Zerubbabel, some of course settled in Jerusalem and others settled in the surrounding cities.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: It is clear from this word that Nehemiah was a man of prayer. For this reason, after he had organized the guarding of the city and those responsible for it, God guided him to take care of the genealogy of those who were in Jerusalem and Judea.
4- “A register of the genealogy”

This register had been made by Zerubbabel 91 years earlier, that is, in the year 536 BC, when he returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with about fifty thousand people. The register was kept in a treasury, but it differs slightly from the register of genealogy ascribed to Zerubbabel and mentioned in (Ezra 2). Why this difference?
a – A difference in names:

Some persons had two names, one in the original Hebrew and the other acquired during his stay in the captivity according to the kingdom to which he was taken captive, such as Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar in Babylon.
b – A difference in numbers:

Perhaps this is because Zerubbabel made two registers of genealogy, one made in Babylon before he traveled to Jerusalem and the other made in Jerusalem after he arrived there. The difference arose because:
Some people were registered in Babylon but changed their decision to return to Jerusalem and held fast to their possessions in the Babylonian kingdom.
Some were not written in the register but decided to return afterward, and so were written in the register made in Jerusalem.

Moreover, these two registers, one of which Ezra used and the other Nehemiah, were checked against the actual situation, and both Ezra and Nehemiah made corrections in the register of genealogy. It should be noted that there was a period of thirteen years between the return of Ezra and that of Nehemiah: Ezra returned in the year 458 BC, while Nehemiah returned in the year 445 BC. During this period some of the Jews naturally died, which is another reason for the difference between the register of genealogy mentioned here and the other register mentioned.

May you depend on prayer before every task, and even delight in prayer, because it is the means of enjoying divine love and fellowship with it. Then your heart will be at peace, for God will guide you to your good and the good of all around you.
2- “The nobles and the rulers”
These are those in authority among the people: the chief priests, the Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers, who will be mentioned in the following verses.

This shows Nehemiah's success in administration and his love of sharing the work with those in authority, for this leads to the success of undertakings. It also shows that Nehemiah did not monopolize authority.
3- “The genealogy”
Nehemiah took care to make genealogies for those who lived in Jerusalem and Judea for the following reasons:
1- To make sure of the faith of all who were there, so as to be certain that they worshiped God faithfully.
2- Preserving the genealogies was necessary until the coming of the awaited Christ, who would come from the tribe of Judah, as the prophecies said, and indeed from Bethlehem without doubt.
3- To make sure of the lineage of the priests and the Levites, so that they might be dedicated to the service of the Temple, since no one else may share in this service.
4- To know who would dwell in Jerusalem, as is clear in (ch. 11:1).
5- So that each person might know his worth and importance. This signifies the importance of every believer, his place in the heart of God, and his membership in the Church, the Body of Christ.
6- So that, seeing the greatness of their numbers, they might thank God for His blessing upon them.
7- So that Nehemiah might be able to divide the work and the responsibilities among those registered in (Ezra 2).

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: Here Zerubbabel and his helpers are mentioned, twelve in number together with Zerubbabel, and they signify the disciples of Christ. The Nehemiah mentioned here is of course not Nehemiah the king's cupbearer, the writer of this book.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The leaders of the people: these are the names of the leaders of the people who returned from the captivity and the number of individuals belonging to them.

It is noted that three of the families of these leaders took part in building the wall. Parosh, the first of the leaders mentioned, had a son, Pedaiah, who took part in the reading of the book of the Law, besides taking part in building the wall.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: Men of Judah and Benjamin: it is noted that the men of Judah returned to only four cities, namely Bethlehem, Netophah, Kirjath-jearim and Nebo, while they possessed 75 cities to which no one returned, but they remained in the captivity.
The children of the tribe of Benjamin, however, returned to 14 cities mentioned in these verses, although the tribe of Benjamin possessed 30 cities.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The priests: David had divided the priests into twenty-four courses, but none returned from the captivity except priests of only three courses, namely “the children of Jedaiah,” who was the head of the second course, the children of Immer, the head of the sixteenth course, and the children of Harim, the head of the third course, as is mentioned in (1 Chr 24:7, 14, 18). It is noted that the children of Pashur mentioned here belong to the course of Immer, that is, the sixteenth course (Jer 20:1). These three courses multiplied afterward and were divided into twenty-four courses.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers: their number was small, since most of them preferred to remain in the captivity. This shows a spiritual weakness in those who should have hastened to return before others, because they were consecrated to the service of God.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The Nethinim and the children of Solomon's servants: the Nethinim were not of the children of Israel, but they joined the people of God in the days of Joshua and lived with them and shared in gathering wood and drawing water. The children of Solomon's servants likewise were not Jews, but they attached themselves to God and clung to the service of His Temple. All of these loved God so much that they left the captivity and returned to Jerusalem, and God rejoiced in them. They signify the Gentiles whom Christ received and for whose salvation He died, just like the Jews.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: Those who could not prove their genealogy:

The Tirshatha: a Babylonian name meaning “the honorable one,” and the title given to the governor on behalf of the Persian kingdom. The Urim and Thummim: two stones carried by the high priest in order to know God's guidance by them; one was inscribed “yes” and the other “no,” and God would make one of them shine in order to declare His will (Num 27:21). Those who could not prove their genealogies were from the people and from the priests.

Sadly, some of the priests had married women who were not of the seed of the priests or the Levites, or even of the Jews generally, but had married foreign women. One example was a priest who married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name, and this is contrary to the Law.

The Tirshatha, who was either Zerubbabel or Nehemiah, declared that the priests who could not prove their genealogies should not take part in the priestly service, but should wait until God chose a high priest who would carry the Urim and Thummim and inquire concerning them whether they should be received into the priesthood or not.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The total number of those registered: the total number of those who returned from the captivity was 42,360 persons, in addition to 7,582 male and female servants, so that the total of men and women who returned from the captivity was about 50,000 persons.

With those who returned from the captivity there was a number of horses, mules, camels and donkeys, amounting to 8,136. These numbers are small compared with those who remained in the captivity, and this shows the weakness of faith and repentance among the Jews. Bondage did not lead them to repentance and return to God; rather, most of them were absorbed in the desires of the world and did not care to return to Jerusalem to worship God.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The Water Gate: it lies to the southeast of Jerusalem and leads to the river Gihon, which is the main source of the water that supplies Jerusalem.

After the wall was completed in the sixth month (ch. 6:15), and the guarding and the genealogies had been arranged, the whole Jewish people gathered with one heart. This was at the beginning of the seventh month, as we said about the last verse of the previous chapter, because this day is a feast well known among them, the Feast of Trumpets, also called the Feast of Shouting (Lev 23:23-25, Num 29:1-6). In this feast they would leave their work and devote themselves to the worship of God. In addition, the Jews used to keep a feast on the first of every month (Num 10:10). The gathering of the people on this feast shows that Ezra had succeeded, over the past 13 years, in teaching the people to worship God and to hold fast to the holy feasts, so that they gathered in Jerusalem of their own accord and not because anyone summoned them. They had seen the work of God and His help to them in building the wall of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah, and so they took care to come to offer holy worship to God on this feast.
The people gathered in the square in Jerusalem, before the Water Gate, because it was a large square that could hold the great numbers of the people, whom the court of the Temple could not hold.

The gathering of the people as one man shows the unity that appeared after the return from the captivity. There was no longer a kingdom of Israel and a kingdom of Judah; rather, the distress of bondage had led them to repentance and the love of God, and so they came forward with one heart to worship Him.

The gathering at the Water Gate signifies the gathering before Christ, the living water, and the Holy Spirit, the fountain of life. Christ declared of Himself that He is the water of life, and that was at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem (Jn 7:37, 38). The Water Gate lies in the east of Jerusalem, and this signifies turning toward the east in prayer, that we may stand before Christ, the fountain of life.

The people's longing for God appeared in their asking Ezra the priest and scribe to read to them the book of the Law of God. This shows the work of Ezra, and after him Nehemiah, in preparing the people, so that they became lovers of God's word and longed to hear it.

What is meant by the book of the Law is not the five books of Moses, but the people's duties toward God and toward one another, which are a part of the book of Deuteronomy and were recorded earlier in the book of Exodus.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: Ezra rejoiced at the spiritual concern that was in the people and at their asking to hear the Law. So he hastened to bring the book of the Law on the Feast of Trumpets, that is, on the first day of the seventh month, to read from it to the multitudes assembled in the square, of men and women, and also the children who had grown up and become able to understand the words of God.

It is known from history that Ezra took care of all the books of the Old Testament (Ezra 7:6, 12), and so he was a student of the Scriptures, especially the book of the Law mentioned in the books of Exodus and Leviticus, a copy of which was kept in the Temple. The Law is the reason for their distinction from the Gentiles, and holding fast to it gives them the power of God which brought them back from the captivity and supported them in building the wall. Therefore they asked to hear the Law, the source of their strength.

It is noted that the high priest Joiakim the son of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, mentioned in (ch. 12:26), is not named in this religious celebration. The reason is not known. It may be because of his illness, or his slackness and negligence, especially since priests of his family had married foreign women (Ezra 10:18); or perhaps he did not appear out of humility and gave the way to Ezra the priest, who was distinguished in the study of the Law.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The people gathered in the morning at the beginning of the day, and Ezra stood and read to them from the book of the Law, most likely quietly so that they could understand the words, and he continued until midday, that is, about twelve noon. This means that he went on reading for a long time, about six hours. That shows how much the people longed to know the word of God and to carry it out.

The people listened with great attention; that is, their ears and their hearts were fixed on the words of God. This shows their love for God and their attachment to Him, contrary to their condition before the captivity, when they neglected the Law, and God allowed them the discipline of the captivity so that they would return to Him.

In proportion to your longing for God's word when you read the Holy Bible, God will reveal to you His love and His mysteries. So be diligent in reading the Holy Bible, and choose a suitable time to read in, so that you may be filled and rejoice.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: Ezra taught the people to care for the feasts and to offer worship to God in them, so it was expected that they would gather on this feast, especially after their victory and their completing the building of the wall. So he prepared a large wooden pulpit, a platform wide enough for a great number to stand upon it, as is mentioned here that fourteen persons stood upon it. It is like the “lectern” found in the Church, but much larger, and it has a place for putting the Holy Bible, in addition to a large place on which the readers stand.

This is the first time the word “pulpit” is mentioned in the Holy Bible. The pulpit was raised above the ground, that is, it was ascended by a ladder, even if only a few steps, so Ezra stood upon it at a level higher than the people, as appears from (v. 5). Six persons stood at Ezra's right hand and seven at his left. Those mentioned were most likely priests, whom Ezra called upon for the following reasons:
1- To show the people the priests' concern for the word of God, so that all the people would feel the reverence due to the Law.
2- They most likely helped Ezra in reading the Law, that is, they took turns in the reading, because it lasted a long time, about six hours, as we mentioned.

3- The standing and reading of these priests who helped Ezra gives them favor in the eyes of the people, and so encourages the priests to read the Law at other times, and the people receive this from them with gladness.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people. It was in the form of a scroll, that is, a piece of skin or paper rolled up, and he opened it, so that it became a large page, in order to begin reading from it.

When Ezra opened the book, the people felt the awe of the word of God, which they were about to hear from Ezra's mouth, and so they all stood in respect and reverence before God. This still happens today in the Church when the “Gospel” is read in the Liturgies and in all the ritual prayers.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: Ezra felt that he was before God when he opened the book, so he blessed God and gave thanks on behalf of all the people, to whom He had given the grace to read and understand His words, since they were His people. It was a grace that the Gentiles did not yet know, but which at that time the people of God alone enjoyed.

When the people felt the presence of God as Ezra prayed and blessed God, all lifted up their hands, sharing with Ezra the feelings of prayer, and said “Amen, Amen,” declaring their sense of the presence of God, as Ezra did. And in deep reverence the whole people bowed down before God, declaring their submission to Him and their readiness to obey His Law.

Therefore the participation of the people in these days in the Church, when they pray, lift up their hands, say “Amen” and bow down before God, declares their response and their love toward God, for the ritual of the Church encourages the people to express their love and submission to God.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: After the book was read on the pulpit, fifteen men, most likely priests, came forward, together with a number of Levites who studied and understood the Law of God, and spread out among the crowds of the people assembled in the square and did the following:

1- They read the Law to them a second time, that is, each person stood with a group and repeated the reading to them, since perhaps their minds had wandered during the reading and they had not grasped some parts.
2- They explained to them the meaning of the Law, that is, they read it distinctly and answered their questions, that is, they made all the people grasp God's purpose in the Law.

3- Some of the people who returned from the captivity had had their language changed, since many Chaldean or Aramaic words had entered it, which they had learned during their stay in the captivity. Their language therefore differed greatly from the Hebrew language in which the Law was written, and so they needed a translation and an explanation of the meaning of the words of the Law.

It is understood from these two verses that the work was very well organized. The people did not move from their places, so that no commotion would arise; rather, the priests and Levites divided the people into groups, and in the midst of each group a person stood to read and explain.
(2) The people's response to the Law (vv. 9-13)

9- And Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha, and Ezra the priest the scribe, and the Levites that taught the people, said unto all the people, This day is holy unto the LORD your God; mourn not, nor weep. For all the people wept, when they heard the words of the law. 10- Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength. 11- So the Levites stilled all the people, saying, Hold your peace, for the day is holy; neither be ye grieved. 12- And all the people went their way to eat, and to drink, and to send portions, and to make great mirth, because they had understood the words that were declared unto them. 13- And on the second day were gathered together the chief of the fathers of all the people, the priests, and the Levites, unto Ezra the scribe, even to understand the words of the law.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The people were pricked in their heart when they heard the words of the Law. They felt their sins and their transgression of the Law of God, and knew that God had disciplined them with the captivity because of their many sins, and had helped them to build the wall because of their return to Him. So they felt their need to hold fast to all the words of the Law, and they wept much. This shows the sensitivity of the people and their repentance and return to God.

But the leaders of the people, namely Nehemiah, Ezra, the priests and the Levites, intervened and asked the people to stop weeping, because the day was a feast of the Lord, in which they ought to rejoice. Thus we find unity of mind among the leaders of the people, so that they were able to calm the crowds on this feast; for the feasts of God are an occasion for joy and there is no weeping in them, except the Day of Atonement, which is a type of the death of Christ the Redeemer, and so they used to weep in it (Lev 23:27). It corresponds to Good Friday in the Church of the New Testament.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The substance of what the leaders, Nehemiah and Ezra, said to the people is as follows:
1- That they should rejoice before God, eat and drink, and thank Him for all His works with them.

2- That they should not forget giving to the needy, who are unable to prepare food for themselves, so that all may share in the joy of the feast. This is what is meant by sending portions to those for whom nothing is prepared, for so it was customary in the feasts of the Lord, and still is today.
3- That they should remember that the day is a holy feast to God and not a time for weeping, but for positive action, which is prayer and helping the needy, as we mentioned.
4- They showed them that joy in the Lord gives them strength, so that they would not fear their enemies, but would go forward in holding fast to the Law of God and in every positive work.
Thank God for His gifts, and rejoice in all the feasts of God and on Sunday, and share the joy with others by helping the needy, encouraging the weak and inviting those far away to the Church.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The Levites, meaning the priests and all the understanding Levites who helped them, assisted Nehemiah and Ezra in calling the people to stop weeping and rejoice in the feast, with all the details mentioned in the preceding verse.
Even today the servants have a great part in the ministry, for they help the bishops and the priests in leading the people along the spiritual way.
And the people obeyed the teachings of their spiritual leaders in all that they said, and this shows the spirituality of the people and the extent of their submission to God.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: All departed on that day, but on the following day the heads of the people, the priests and the Levites returned and gathered to Ezra in submission, to learn from him details of the Law, and perhaps they concerned the Feast of Tabernacles, which is spoken of in the following verses. This shows that the teacher must go on learning humbly throughout his life, and then God works in him with power. It also shows the great spiritual standing of Ezra, for he was the authority in understanding the Law of God.

Likewise the return of the heads and the priests to Ezra shows that whoever loves the word of God and is attached to it longs for more. The more a person reads the words of God, the more he wishes to know than others, and God reveals to him new depths in knowing Him. So after they had spent a whole day in reading the Law of God, their hearts were moved, and on the next day they longed to know more from Ezra.
(3) The Feast of Tabernacles (vv. 14-18)

14- And they found written in the law which the LORD had commanded by Moses, that the children of Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month: 15- And that they should publish and proclaim in all their cities, and in Jerusalem, saying, Go forth unto the mount, and fetch olive branches, and pine branches, and myrtle branches, and palm branches, and branches of thick trees, to make booths, as it is written. 16- So the people went forth, and brought them, and made themselves booths, every one upon the roof of his house, and in their courts, and in the courts of the house of God, and in the street of the water gate, and in the street of the gate of Ephraim.

17- And all the congregation of them that were come again out of the captivity made booths, and sat under the booths: for since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun unto that day had not the children of Israel done so. And there was very great gladness. 18- Also day by day, from the first day unto the last day, he read in the book of the law of God. And they kept the feast seven days; and on the eighth day was a solemn assembly, according unto the manner.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: When they read the book of the Law, they found that they ought to keep a feast in the seventh month, the Feast of Tabernacles. So searching in the word of God teaches a person how to worship Him.
The Jews had seven feasts, which are:
1- The Feast of the Passover
2- The Feast of Unleavened Bread
3- The Feast of Firstfruits
4- The Feast of Pentecost
5- The Feast of Trumpets
6- The Feast of Atonement

7- The Feast of Tabernacles. There were three great feasts at which all the men had to come to Jerusalem to stand before the Temple of God, namely the feasts of the Passover, Pentecost and the Harvest.

It is noted that the last three feasts are celebrated in the seventh month: Trumpets on the first day, Atonement on the tenth day, and Tabernacles from the fifteenth day to the twenty-second. The Feast of Tabernacles coincides with the time of gathering the summer harvests, and so it is a day of joy in the Lord and His blessings and gifts.

In the Feast of Tabernacles all the Jews go out from their dwellings and set up booths, that is, huts or shelters, for seven days, and on the eighth day there is a solemn assembly. This is for the following reasons:

1- To remember the days of their sojourning in the wilderness of Sinai, so that they live in the spirit of being strangers to the world and do not cling to the material things and goods of the land of Canaan.
2- So that they might feel unity, since the rich and the poor all live in booths which they make on the roofs of their houses or in the squares.
3- So that the rich might feel for the poor and their needs, and help them.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: Myrtle: a fragrant evergreen tree, small in size.
Thick: dense.
The Law commanded the people to go out to the mountain and gather branches of various trees, in order to make their booths with them.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The Gate of Ephraim: it is in the western wall of the city of Jerusalem.

The people obeyed the word of God and made the booths, whether on the roofs of their houses, or in the courts of the Temple and the wide squares of Jerusalem, such as the square of the Water Gate and the square of Ephraim.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: The people kept the Feast of Tabernacles with all exactness, and the like had not been done since the days of Joshua the son of Nun. For the keeping of the Feast of Tabernacles in the days of Solomon (1 Kgs 8:65, 66) and in the days of Ezra (Ezra 3:4), despite its greatness, was not as exact as what they did in the days of Nehemiah. In the days of Solomon the feast was great, but they did not hold a solemn assembly on the eighth day.

The people rejoiced greatly at carrying out the word of God. When they repented of their sins and wept, they rejoiced and ate, and then remembered their being strangers to the world through the Feast of Tabernacles. Such is the effect of listening to the word of God and submitting to it.

entries.section: (3) The gift to the Temple

paragraphs.text: Ezra, the priests and the Levites took care, in this Feast of Tabernacles, to read from the book of the Law every day, for the people who dwelt in the booths came every morning before the Temple of God and listened to the book of the Law.

Remember that you are a stranger in the world, so that you are not occupied with love of possessions, are not troubled by any loss, are forgiving toward others, and think of eternity, and so live with God in good fellowship.

Fasting and the prayer of praise: on the Feast of Trumpets, on the first day of the seventh month, sorrow was mingled with joy (ch. 8), when the people wept at hearing the book of the Law, and Nehemiah and Ezra called them to rejoice on this great day. After the celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles from the fifteenth to the twenty-second day of the seventh month, they returned to their houses, and then came back on the twenty-fourth day to gather and offer repentance with sorrow, and then joy in praising God.
In the ninth chapter of this book we find a prayer that includes repentance and praise, as we find the same meaning in the ninth chapter of both the books of Ezra and Daniel.

entries.section: (1) Fasting and repentance

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel gathered of themselves out of love for God, on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month. The place where they gathered is not mentioned, but it was most likely before the house of God, where the priests, the Levites and the books of the Holy Bible were.

They sanctified a fast on this day, a voluntary fast not prescribed by the Law of Moses. By this fast they drew near to God. We shall notice in the rest of this chapter that they thanked God and praised Him, and so joy was mingled with sorrow, as happened on the Feast of Trumpets, because holy sorrow in repentance gives peace, just as joy is also accompanied by inner peace. Even today sorrow is mingled with joy in the sacrament of confession, for repentance is accompanied by spiritual joy in God. Fasts, too, are always joined to prayers.

This fast was joined with humbling before God, for they put on sackcloth, which is coarse clothing, and put dust on their heads, remembering their sins; that is, they humbled themselves before God. Humbling in fasting makes it acceptable before God, as the prophet Isaiah said (Isa 58:5). In this voluntary fast, which the Law did not mention, we see a support for what the Apostles and the Fathers did when they appointed fasts which the Church keeps to this day, although Christ mentioned only the idea of fasting and Himself fasted for us. God gives us the idea of fasting and waits for us to respond to Him. This is what the Church did, appointing its various fasts throughout the year.

entries.section: (1) Fasting and repentance

paragraphs.text: The second condition that Isaiah mentioned for an acceptable fast was fulfilled here by the people, namely breaking the bonds of evil. They separated themselves from the foreign women, as the Law prescribed; that is, they kept away from everything that bound them to idolatrous worship, that they might live in purity before God.

The book of Ezra (Ezra 9) tells us that Ezra was greatly distressed when he heard that the people had joined themselves to foreign women. Perhaps they had separated from them at that time, but afterward went back and joined themselves to them again; and here, when they fasted, they separated once more from these foreign women.

The third condition for an acceptable fast they fulfilled by their confession of their sins, and by this they obtained God's mercies, as David mentioned in (Ps 32:5) when he confessed his sin, and likewise Job when he confessed before all (Job 31:34). We notice here two kinds of confession: a common confession of the people before God, besides a personal confession before the priest, when the person laid his hand on the sacrifice and then the priest slew it on his behalf.

entries.section: (1) Fasting and repentance

paragraphs.text: The fourth condition for an acceptable fast is the reading of the word of God, and they read in the book of the Law of the Lord, sitting quietly and listening to the word of God for a fourth part of the day, which is about three hours, since the day is about 12 hours, from six in the morning to six in the evening. Perhaps they would read a portion, and then the priests and Levites would explain it to the people, and there may have been an opportunity to answer the people's questions. It is also possible that they read to all, then divided them into groups, and then one of the Levites or priests sat down to explain to them according to their language and to answer their questions, as we mentioned in (ch. 8:8). It appears that the humbling of the people, their separation from the foreign wives and their confession of sin helped them to approach the word of God and to listen to it with attention.
Likewise the people's listening to the book of the Law at the Feast of Shouting, and then during the days of the Feast of Tabernacles, stirred their longing to ask to listen to the word of God.

The fifth condition for an acceptable fast is prayer, for the crowds assembled, after their reading in the Law, spent the second fourth of the day, about three hours, in glorifying God and bowing down to Him, that is, prayers of thanksgiving and praise to God joined with humility through prostrations (metanoias).
Listening to the word of God and meditating on it moves the heart to prayer, whether in thanksgiving and praise, or in humility and repentance.

The prayers of thanksgiving and glorification came from their sense of the mercy of God, who received them when they confessed their sins and humbled themselves before Him; for repentance increases by reading the word of God, and it moves the heart to thanksgiving and worship. Although it is mentioned that they spent a fourth of the day in reading and the second fourth in prayer, perhaps they repeated this, that is, they read in the third fourth and prayed in the fourth, so that they continued all day, twelve hours, in reading and prayer. This variety in the spiritual portions helped them not to grow weary, and therefore to enjoy being with God for a long time. This is what the children of God need to this day, whether those who worship God in the world, or in the wilderness, and also the solitaries.

God rejoices in your fasting and your drawing near to Him, so always join your fasting with humility, repentance, reading and prayer, and you will taste the sweetness of fellowship with God and rejoice in fasting. Your God has fasted on your behalf, and He must sit with you, so do not be slow to hasten to Him.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: Eight of the Levites stood upon the stairs, that is, a raised platform with steps, so as to be at a higher level than the people, so that they could easily be seen and heard at the time of prayer and the reading of the holy Scriptures. Perhaps this platform is the very one that they prepared and used on the Feast of Shouting, on which Ezra and thirteen of the priests stood (ch. 8:4), or perhaps it was another pulpit in the Temple.
When these Levites, among whom there may have been priests, stood, they prayed in a loud voice from their depths, so that the Holy Bible expressed it by saying that they “cried.”

These eight prayed on the pulpit, either all with one voice, or one after another in turn. It is also possible that they divided the assembled people into eight parts, and each of the Levites led a group of the people in prayer.
The number eight signifies eternity, for these Levites by their prayers lift up the hearts of the people to life with God and the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: As the Levites felt the warmth of prayer, they wished to share the people with them, so they called them to stand up and pray with them and bless God. This prayer is thanksgiving and praise.
The Levites asked the people to praise God, the Eternal, the Everlasting, because He is above all gods and all creatures.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: The Levites declared (and the Septuagint translation says that the speaker was Ezra, the spiritual leader of the people), and in their glorification of God they proclaimed that He is the one God, the Creator of all beings in heaven and on earth. He is worthy of glorification by all, not because He is in need, but because this is the natural feeling of all His creatures, that they should glorify Him.

In this prayer they declared not only that He is the one God and the Creator of all, but also that He gives life to all creatures; He is the secret of their continuance, and therefore glorifying Him is a duty, because He is the secret of the life of all His creatures.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: Ur of the Chaldees: a city situated in the south of Mesopotamia, in Iraq.

The prayer here began with thanking God for His works with His people, after they had glorified God, blessed by all His creation. In these two verses they blessed God for His choosing of Abram, the father of the people of God. This choosing is a free divine grace which God grants to those who love Him, for Abram worshiped God although idolatry was spread around him in the whole world.
Out of the love of God He brought Abram out from the midst of his people, who had begun to be defiled by idolatry, in order to keep him alone in the wilderness in the right faith.
And God's love added a new grace for Abram by changing his name to Abraham, so that he might feel the following:
1- That he would live a new life to God in purity, better than his former life among his family.

2- Abram means “exalted father,” while Abraham means “father of a great multitude.” The change of his name was thus good news to him that he would be the father of a great people who believe in God, the people of the children of Israel.

God also gave a grace to Abraham, namely the covenant which He made with him because of his faithfulness in the worship of God. He promised him that he would inherit and possess the whole land of Canaan, in which six idolatrous peoples dwelt. And God fulfilled His promise, for the seed of Abraham possessed this land in the days of Joshua.

God is true and faithful in fulfilling His promises, and human beings respond to Him according to their faith and love. Seldom is it said of a man that he is faithful, but faithfulness is mentioned of Moses and Abraham.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: The Red Sea (Yam Suph): the Red Sea.
“Dealt proudly against them”: they did evil to them, that is, they wronged them.
“Thou didst divide the sea”: You split the sea.

After thanking God for His choosing of Abraham, they thank God for His care of His people the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians humbled. When they cried out to God, He sent them Moses and struck Egypt with great wonders, the ten plagues, by which He showed the weakness of their idolatrous gods, confirmed the faith of His people, and called the Egyptians to faith.

After the people of God had gone out of Egypt and reached the Red Sea, Pharaoh turned back and went out after them, to bring them back as slaves to him, to serve him in building cities and in every work. They cried out to God, and then He divided the Red Sea for them, which had been an obstacle to them in their flight, and made it a road through which they fled to the wilderness of Sinai. And the pillar of fire stood between them and the Egyptians and protected them.

When Pharaoh hardened his heart and followed the people of God into the sea, God brought His people out into the wilderness of Sinai and overwhelmed Pharaoh and all his army with water in the sea, so that they all died. God became a glorified name among all the peoples of the world, who heard of this great miracle, so all the peoples feared Him and some of them believed in Him, like Rahab.

The thanksgiving to God for delivering them from the Egyptians is remembered by the people now because God delivered them from the bondage of Babylon: He overthrew Babylon and the kingdom of the Medes and Persians took its place, which sent the people of God back to their land, and they built the Temple and Jerusalem and worshiped Him with joy.
The name of God was glorified through Pharaoh, and is glorified today through the building of the wall of Jerusalem, despite the obstinacy of the enemies.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: After God delivered His people from the bondage of Egypt, they held fast to Him and asked His guidance in the vast wilderness of Sinai. So He sent them a pillar of cloud by day to overshadow them, which turned at night into a pillar of fire to give them light.

The pillar of cloud or the pillar of fire was not only a guide for the movements of the people of God, but a sign of the presence of God, which reassured them and made their hearts joyful, so they glorified God and blessed Him.

Perhaps the people's remembering God's guidance of them in the wilderness of Sinai was an incentive for them to seek God's guidance in their conduct and in their life with Him and with those around them, after He had reassured them by the building of the wall of Jerusalem.

It is good that you remember God's gifts and kindnesses and thank Him for them, for this shows your appreciation of God's love and urges you to enjoy His care more than before, so that your heart always rejoices.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: God's love appeared in His spiritual care of His people. After He separated them from the idolatrous peoples, He Himself came down upon Mount Sinai and gave them His commandments and laws, that they might live by them. He also sanctified the Sabbath day that they might worship Him on it every week. They lived in these laws and commandments every day, every week and throughout the year, and by these good teachings they were distinguished from the rest of the idolatrous peoples of the world and enjoyed the presence of God in their midst. Moses was their spiritual leader, who received all these teachings from God in order to guide them in the straight way.

entries.section: (2) Thanksgiving to God who rescued His people from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: God also cared for their material needs. He gave them in a miraculous way food every day from heaven and also water from the rock wherever they went, so that they lacked nothing for forty years. God also promised them the inheritance of the land of Canaan, which overflows with many good things, after they should complete their journey in the wilderness of Sinai.

Thus we see complete care from God and inexpressible love, and thus His people lacked nothing. This is the love of God. But what, one wonders, was the people's reaction? Sadly it was bad, as we shall see in the following verses.

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people

paragraphs.text: “Dealt proudly”: they wronged God, that is, they rebelled against Him.
“Hardened their necks”: when an animal stiffens its neck it refuses to submit to the work of drawing farm implements, and the phrase means rebellion.

The people's reaction was very strange, the very opposite of what was expected. Instead of thanking God and worshiping Him faithfully like Moses, they rebelled against God, refusing to submit to His commandments, and they also refused to listen to His Law and to the guidance of Moses to them, that they should return to God. In addition to that, they forgot God's wonders with them, whether in bringing them out of the land of Egypt or in caring for them in the wilderness of Sinai. And the hardest of all this was that they preferred bondage in Egypt to life with God, so they appointed a leader in place of Moses to lead them back to Egypt.

What is wonderful is God's longsuffering toward His people and His great mercy: He did not forsake them, but gave them an opportunity for repentance and led them about in the wilderness of Sinai, and when they were partly sorry for their sins, He forgave them and went on caring for them in the wilderness, because in truth He is a gracious and compassionate God.

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people

paragraphs.text: Despite God's mercy, His people went back to rebelling against Him. While He was giving them the commandments and the Law and the pattern of the tabernacle of meeting, that He might dwell in their midst by the hand of Moses, they made a god for themselves, a golden calf, to worship instead of God, imitating the idolatrous nations around them.

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people

paragraphs.text: In the face of all this rebellion and evil, God's mercy and care for His people in the wilderness continued. He led them by the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night; that is, He remained present with them and their leader. God's spiritual care for His children continued: He did not withdraw from them His commandments and Law, but His Holy Spirit continued to guide them through these commandments and teachings by the hand of Moses, the priests, the Levites and the elders of the people (Num 11:24-25). God's care also continued in feeding them manna and giving them water from the rock.

We see here the people, who are praying on this day, repeating their thanksgiving to God for His care by the pillar of cloud and fire, the commandments, the manna and the water, because God's care was not affected by the evil of their fathers; rather, God remained good and faithful to His people despite all their rebellion.

The wonder also appeared in God's care when He preserved their clothes and their sandals for forty years in the wilderness, and also preserved their feet, so that they did not swell from much walking in the desert.

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people

paragraphs.text: During their journey in the wilderness they met peoples east of the Dead Sea, before they crossed the Jordan and entered the land of Canaan. They triumphed over them by the power of God and possessed their land; these were Sihon and Og, the great kings, kings of the Amorites.

Thus the power of God is made manifest, who worked with His people, who were shepherds of sheep untrained for war. They triumphed over strong kings and scattered in many directions to possess wide lands east of the river Jordan, such as Heshbon and Bashan, under the leadership of Moses the prophet, before their entering the land of Canaan.

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people

paragraphs.text: In God's care for His people, He multiplied their children, preserved their lives and gave them strength, so that they were able to enter the land of Canaan and seize its fortified cities, such as Jericho, and possess its wide lands full of good things. It was planted with vineyards and full of wells that gave water abundantly (Deut 9:3, Deut 7:24; Josh 11:12, 17; Judg 1:4). So Your people enjoyed abundant delights which You gave them, for which they had not labored in planting and building.

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people

paragraphs.text: Sadly the fathers did not thank God for all these many gifts, but disobeyed His commandments and left His Law, and when God sent prophets to them to bring them back to Him, they rejected the word of God and rose up against the prophets and killed them, like Isaiah, whom they sawed in two with a wooden saw, and Jeremiah, whom they stoned (Heb 11:37).

entries.section: (3) The longsuffering of God toward His rebellious people
